docs.title: Home Compute Cluster
docs.text:
A three-node bare-metal K3s platform, built to learn how real infrastructure is actually operated.

Not a toy repo, not a cloud tutorial. A standing homelab where GitOps, distributed storage, observability, and hand-rolled networking run on hardware I own, so the mistakes are cheap and the lessons are real.

Read the motivation Jump to architecture

docs.title: The rundown
docs.text:
• Why this exists

    The career and learning case for owning the hardware, and the alternatives (cloud, single box, Pi cluster) that lost the argument.

    Motivation

  • Architecture

    Node inventory, network topology, GitOps control loop, and the split public / tailnet ingress model, with diagrams.

    System design

  • CI / CD

    The git push -> build -> deploy loop. GitHub Actions to ghcr.io, ArgoCD reconciling the cluster to match Git.

    Pipeline

  • K3s & containers

    How the cluster is stood up and how workloads get packaged and scheduled across heterogeneous nodes.

    K3s guide

docs.title: The rig
docs.text:
Three heterogeneous, always-on x86 nodes. The names stuck, so they stayed.

Node Callsign Hardware Role deus control plane Lenovo M910q K3s server, ingress brain, ArgoCD nebula worker + NAS i7-6700K, GTX 1080 ZFS storage, Seafile, Longhorn replica legion worker Laptop, GTX 1060 Longhorn replica, MetalLB VIP advertiser

Stack: K3s · ArgoCD · Traefik · MetalLB · Longhorn · ZFS · Prometheus · Grafana · Cloudflare Tunnel · Tailscale · WireGuard

Domains: *.packetcraft.dev (public) · *.lab.packetcraft.dev (tailnet-only)

docs.text:
New here? Read the motivation for the why, then the architecture for the how. If you just want to follow the build as it happened, the weekly logs are the running diary.

The value is in the decision log, not the uptime number. Every choice here has a reason, and the reason is written down.

docs.title: GitOps for Off-the-Shelf Software — Setup Guide
docs.text:
A companion to cicd-pipeline-setup-guide.md. That guide covers built-from-source services (you write the code, CI builds an image). This one covers off-the-shelf software you don't compile — Grafana, Jellyfin, Longhorn, cert-manager, anything that already ships an image or a Helm chart.

The key difference: off-the-shelf software has no app repo and no CI. There is nothing to build. You only declare what to run; ArgoCD reconciles the cluster to match. This is the CD applies to everything you run; CI only applies to things you build rule from the main guide — here, CI is simply absent.

docs.title: 1. Which of the two patterns applies?
docs.text:
Off-the-shelf software arrives in one of two shapes. Pick the pattern that matches how the software is distributed.

Shape Example Pattern A plain container image Jellyfin, a public nginx, linuxserver.io images Pattern A — raw manifests A Helm chart kube-prometheus-stack, Longhorn, cert-manager, ArgoCD itself Pattern B — ArgoCD Application pointing at a Helm chart

Rule of thumb: if the project's install docs say "here's our image, write your own Deployment," use Pattern A. If they say "helm install ...," use Pattern B — never hand-translate a chart into raw manifests, you lose every upstream default and every future upgrade.

docs.title: 2. Pattern A — raw manifests for a plain image
docs.text: Identical to the source-built layout in the main guide, minus the app repo and the images: tag-bump seam (there's no CI to bump it — you pin the version yourself).

docs.title: Config repo layout
docs.text:
homelab-cicd-config/
└── apps/
    └── jellyfin/
        ├── kustomization.yaml
        ├── deployment.yaml
        └── service.yaml

docs.title: deployment.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jellyfin
  namespace: jellyfin
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jellyfin
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: jellyfin
    spec:
      # placement: pin to wherever the workload belongs (GPU node, storage node…)
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: nebula
      containers:
        - name: jellyfin
          image: jellyfin/jellyfin:10.9.11   # PIN A VERSION — never :latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8096

docs.title: service.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: jellyfin
  namespace: jellyfin
spec:
  selector:
    app: jellyfin
  ports:
    - port: 8096
      targetPort: 8096

docs.title: kustomization.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: jellyfin
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml

No images: block needed — there's no CI rewriting a tag. You set the version in deployment.yaml by hand and commit it. Renovate (already on your roadmap) watches these pinned tags and opens a PR when jellyfin/jellyfin:10.9.12 ships, so upgrades stay declarative: review PR → merge → ArgoCD rolls it.

docs.title: ArgoCD Application
docs.text:
Same as any service (from the main guide §6):

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: jellyfin
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/BarneyLaw/homelab-cicd-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/jellyfin
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: jellyfin
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

docs.title: 3. Pattern B — ArgoCD Application pointing at a Helm chart
docs.text:
This is the important one, because most serious off-the-shelf infra ships as a chart, and it's how Grafana already arrived on your cluster (via kube-prometheus-stack). The mistake to avoid: helm install by hand. That puts the release outside Git — exactly the drift that bit the Grafana lab. IngressRoute.

ArgoCD renders Helm charts itself. You point an Application at the chart and supply values; ArgoCD templates it and reconciles the output. The chart's release is now owned by Git, upgrades are a values/version change in a commit, and self-heal applies.

docs.title: Two ways to feed values
docs.text:
B1 — inline values in the Application (fine for small overrides):

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: kube-prometheus-stack
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
    chart: kube-prometheus-stack
    targetRevision: 65.1.1            # PIN the chart version
    helm:
      values: |
        grafana:
          enabled: true
          # values that used to live in your hand-run `helm install`
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: monitoring
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - ServerSideApply=true          # big CRD-heavy charts need this

B2 — values file in the config repo (better once values grow; this is the clean long-term shape). Use a multi-source Application: one source is the upstream chart, the other is your repo holding the values file.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: kube-prometheus-stack
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  sources:
    - repoURL: https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
      chart: kube-prometheus-stack
      targetRevision: 65.1.1
      helm:
        valueFiles:
          - $values/apps/kube-prometheus-stack/values.yaml
    - repoURL: https://github.com/BarneyLaw/homelab-cicd-config.git
      targetRevision: main
      ref: values                     # makes $values resolve to this repo
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: monitoring
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - ServerSideApply=true

Config repo gains:

homelab-cicd-config/
└── apps/
    └── kube-prometheus-stack/
        └── values.yaml      # everything you'd have passed to `helm install`

Migrating an already-hand-installed chart (your Grafana case): point a Pattern B Application at the same chart + version you currently have installed, with your current values. On first sync ArgoCD adopts the existing release rather than duplicating it, provided chart name, version, namespace, and release name line up. Pin targetRevision to the version you actually have now (find it with helm list -A), sync, confirm Healthy, then bump the version in a later commit. Don't combine "adopt" and "upgrade" in one move — you won't know which broke what.

docs.title: Where the Grafana lab. IngressRoute belongs now
docs.text:
Two clean homes, pick one:

  1. In the chart values — kube-prometheus-stack exposes grafana.extraObjects (or you template the IngressRoute through the chart), so the lab. IngressRoute is rendered by the same Application. Most cohesive.
  2. As a sibling raw manifest — a small apps/monitoring-extras/ folder (Pattern A, manifests only, no Deployment) holding just the Grafana IngressRoute, with its own ArgoCD Application. Simpler to reason about; keeps "the chart" and "my routing for the chart" as separate Applications.

Either way the hand-applied IngressRoute stops being an orphan. Given you already have it applied, the lowest-friction path is option 2: drop the YAML you already wrote into apps/monitoring-extras/, add an Application, and ArgoCD adopts it.

docs.title: 4. Decision flow (the whole thing in one place)
docs.text:
New software to run?
│
├─ Do you write its source code?
│   ├─ YES → main guide (app repo + CI + config repo). CI builds & bumps tag.
│   └─ NO  → this guide (config repo only, no CI):
│           │
│           ├─ Distributed as a Helm chart?
│           │   ├─ YES → Pattern B (ArgoCD App → chart + pinned version + values)
│           │   │         small values → B1 inline; growing values → B2 values file
│           │   └─ NO (plain image) → Pattern A (raw manifests, pinned tag)
│           │
│           └─ Keep upgrades declarative with Renovate watching pinned versions.

docs.title: 5. Off-the-shelf checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Decide Pattern A (image) vs B (chart). When in doubt, follow how upstream tells you to install it.
  • [ ] Pin the version — image tag (A) or targetRevision chart version (B). Never :latest, never an unpinned chart.
  • [ ] Add apps/<service>/ to homelab-cicd-config (manifests, or chart values).
  • [ ] Create the ArgoCD Application (commit it into the repo too, e.g. argocd/<service>.yaml, for reproducibility).
  • [ ] For charts: add ServerSideApply=true if it's CRD-heavy (prometheus stack, Longhorn, cert-manager all qualify).
  • [ ] Confirm Synced / Healthy, pods Running.
  • [ ] (Optional) tunnel hostname + IngressRoute for public, or lab. IngressRoute
    • grey-cloud Cloudflare A record for tailnet-only.
  • [ ] Let Renovate watch the pinned version for upgrade PRs.

docs.title: 6. Common failure modes (additions to the main guide's table)
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Chart sync fails on CRDs / the server could not find the requested resource giant chart applied client-side; CRDs too big for annotations add ServerSideApply=true to syncOptions ArgoCD duplicates a chart you helm installed by hand release name / namespace / version don't match the existing release align all three to the live release (helm list -A) so ArgoCD adopts, not re-creates Hand-applied manifest vanishes after a helm upgrade the object lived outside Git, inside a chart-managed namespace move it into the config repo as a tracked manifest or into chart values :latest silently changed under you unpinned image tag pin an explicit version; let Renovate PR upgrades Application stuck OutOfSync on a chart's own mutated fields chart writes fields back (webhooks, defaulting) add the noisy fields to ignoreDifferences on the Application

docs.title: GitOps CI/CD Pipeline — Setup Guide
docs.text:
A reusable template for wiring any custom-built service into the homelab's git push → build → deploy pipeline. Built around GitHub Actions (CI) + ArgoCD/Kustomize (CD) on K3s, with cloudflared + Traefik for ingress.

The nginx test workload is used throughout as the worked example. To stand up a new service, copy the structure and substitute the placeholders marked <like-this>.

docs.title: 1. Mental model (read once)
docs.text:
The pipeline has two halves that never talk to each other directly. They communicate only through the config repo.

  ┌──────────────┐  push code   ┌─────────────────┐
  │  app repo    │ ───────────▶ │ GitHub Actions  │   CI
  │ (source+CI)  │              │ build + push    │   (GitHub-hosted runner)
  └──────────────┘              └────────┬────────┘
                                         │ 1. push image:SHA
                                         ▼
                                   ┌───────────┐
                                   │  ghcr.io  │
                                   └───────────┘
                                         │ 2. write SHA into manifest
                                         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐ ArgoCD watches ┌─────────────┐
  │ config repo  │ ◀───────────── │  kustomize  │
  │ (manifests)  │                │  edit image │
  └──────┬───────┘                └─────────────┘
         │ 3. reconcile
         ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ ArgoCD (in-cluster, always-on)│ ──▶ Deployment rolls to image:SHA   CD
  └──────────────────────────────┘
  • CI (GitHub runner): turns a commit into a tested, versioned image and publishes it. Then writes the new image tag into the config repo. Has no cluster access.
  • CD (ArgoCD, inside the cluster): watches the config repo and reconciles the cluster to match it. Pulls desired state; nothing pushes into the cluster from outside.

Key rule: CD applies to everything you run; CI only applies to things you build. Off-the-shelf images (Jellyfin, Grafana) skip CI entirely — they need only a config-repo manifest + an ArgoCD Application.

docs.title: 2. Two-repo layout
docs.text:
Always use two repos. One repo causes an infinite loop (CI's write-back re-triggers CI).

Repo Role Who writes Who reads <service>-app Source + CI workflow You (humans) GitHub Actions homelab-cicd-config K8s manifests GitHub Actions (bot) ArgoCD

The config repo is shared across all services — each service gets its own subfolder under apps/.

docs.title: App repo layout
docs.text:
<service>-app/
├── Dockerfile
├── <app source files>
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── build.yaml

docs.title: Config repo layout (grows per service)
docs.text:
homelab-cicd-config/
└── apps/
    ├── nginx/
    │   ├── kustomization.yaml
    │   ├── deployment.yaml
    │   └── service.yaml
    └── <service>/
        ├── kustomization.yaml
        ├── deployment.yaml
        └── service.yaml

docs.title: 3. Config repo: the three manifest files
docs.text: Per service, under apps/<service>/.

docs.title: deployment.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: <service>
  namespace: <service>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: <service>
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: <service>
    spec:
      # Pin to the always-on control-plane node (deus = the M910q).
      # Omit or change for GPU/storage-bound workloads.
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: deus
      containers:
        - name: <service>
          image: ghcr.io/<owner-lowercase>/<service>-app:latest  # tag rewritten by CI
          ports:
            - containerPort: <port>

docs.title: service.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: <service>
  namespace: <service>
spec:
  selector:
    app: <service>
  ports:
    - port: <port>
      targetPort: <port>

docs.title: kustomization.yaml
docs.text:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: <service>
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml
images:
  - name: ghcr.io/<owner-lowercase>/<service>-app
    newTag: latest   # CI overwrites this line via `kustomize edit set image`

The images: block is the seam. CI runs kustomize edit set image which surgically rewrites newTag here. You never hand-edit the deployment's image line.

docs.title: Gotchas that cause silent failures
docs.text:
• Filenames matter. Kustomize specifically reads the file named kustomization.yaml. Don't swap file contents.
  • ghcr.io is all-lowercase. <owner-lowercase> must be lowercase even if your GitHub login has capitals (BarneyLaw → barneylaw). kustomize edit set image does a case-sensitive string match — a case mismatch matches nothing and the tag silently never updates.

docs.title: 4. App repo: the CI workflow
docs.text:
.github/workflows/build.yaml. Substitute <service> and confirm the config repo name.

name: build-and-update-config
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write          # lets the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN push to ghcr.io
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout app repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Log in to ghcr.io
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push image
        id: build
        run: |
          # force lowercase owner — ghcr.io rejects uppercase repo names
          IMAGE=ghcr.io/$(echo ${{ github.repository_owner }} | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')/<service>-app
          SHA=${GITHUB_SHA::7}
          docker build -t $IMAGE:$SHA -t $IMAGE:latest .
          docker push $IMAGE:$SHA
          docker push $IMAGE:latest
          echo "image=$IMAGE" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "sha=$SHA" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Checkout config repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          repository: ${{ github.repository_owner }}/homelab-cicd-config
          token: ${{ secrets.CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN }}
          path: config

      - name: Install kustomize
        run: |
          curl -s "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/kustomize/master/hack/install_kustomize.sh" | bash
          sudo mv kustomize /usr/local/bin/

      - name: Bump image tag
        working-directory: config/apps/<service>
        run: |
          kustomize edit set image ${{ steps.build.outputs.image }}=${{ steps.build.outputs.image }}:${{ steps.build.outputs.sha }}

      - name: Commit and push tag bump
        working-directory: config
        run: |
          git config user.name  "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add apps/<service>/kustomization.yaml
          git commit -m "deploy: <service> ${{ steps.build.outputs.sha }}" || echo "no changes"
          git push

Image is tagged by short SHA (immutable, traceable) and latest (convenience). ArgoCD deploys the SHA, so every deploy is pinned to an exact build.

docs.title: 5. Credentials (the part that's easy to get wrong)
docs.text:
Three boundaries, each needs its own credential only when it crosses into private. Scope every credential to the minimum.

Boundary Credential Who creates it Needed when CI → ghcr.io (push image) GITHUB_TOKEN (auto) + packages: write GitHub, automatic always (just declare the permission) CI → config repo (write tag) CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN (fine-grained PAT) You, by hand always (cross-repo write) Cluster → ghcr.io (pull image) image pull secret You only if package is private ArgoCD → config repo (read) repo creds You only if config repo is private

docs.title: Creating CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN (one-time, reusable across all services)
docs.text:
1. GitHub → avatar → Settings → Developer settings.
  2. Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token.
  3. Repository access: Only select repositories → homelab-cicd-config.
  4. Permissions: Repository permissions → Contents → Read and write. Nothing else.
  5. Generate, copy the github_pat_... value.
  6. In each <service>-app repo → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret. Name: CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN, value: the token.

One PAT scoped to the config repo works for every app repo, since they all write to the same config repo. Add it as a secret in each app repo.

docs.title: Private package → image pull secret
docs.text:
If the ghcr package is private (default), the cluster can't pull. Either make it public (Package → settings → Change visibility → Public), or:

kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-pull \
  --namespace <service> \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=<owner> \
  --docker-password=<PAT-with-read:packages>

then add to the deployment pod spec:

    spec:
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: ghcr-pull

docs.title: Private config repo → ArgoCD repo creds
docs.text:
argocd repo add https://github.com/<owner>/homelab-cicd-config.git \
  --username <owner> \
  --password <PAT-with-repo-read>

docs.title: 6. CD: the ArgoCD Application
docs.text:
Per service. Save as <service>-app.yaml, apply with kubectl apply -f. For full GitOps, also commit this into the config repo (e.g. argocd/<service>.yaml) so ArgoCD's own app definitions are reproducible.

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: <service>
  namespace: argocd          # the Application object lives in argocd's namespace
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/<owner>/homelab-cicd-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/<service>     # the folder ArgoCD watches
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc   # "this cluster"
    namespace: <service>     # where the workload's pods land
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true            # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true         # revert manual drift back to Git's state
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true # create the namespace if absent

kubectl apply -f <service>-app.yaml

repoURL is the entire Gitea migration later — switch this one line to the Gitea URL, re-add repo creds, done.

docs.title: 7. Ingress (optional, for externally-reachable services)
docs.text:
Architecture: cloudflared (systemd on deus) → Traefik (localhost:80) → IngressRoute → service. The tunnel is a dumb pipe; Traefik is the routing brain.

  1. Add a public hostname to the deus tunnel in Cloudflare: <service>.packetcraft.dev → http://localhost:80. Cloudflare auto-creates a proxied CNAME and terminates TLS at its edge (real cert — required because .dev is HSTS-preloaded and rejects self-signed).
  2. Create a Traefik IngressRoute:
apiVersion: traefik.io/v1alpha1
kind: IngressRoute
metadata:
  name: <service>
  namespace: <service>
spec:
  entryPoints:
    - web
  routes:
    - match: Host(`<service>.packetcraft.dev`)
      kind: Rule
      services:
        - name: <service>
          port: <port>

Every new externally-exposed service = one CNAME (public hostname on the tunnel) + one IngressRoute. The tunnel config itself never changes again.

If the app serves its own TLS / redirects to HTTPS internally (e.g. ArgoCD), run it in insecure/HTTP mode so Traefik+Cloudflare own TLS, or you get a redirect loop.

docs.title: 8. End-to-end test (proves the loop)
docs.text:
# 1. make a visible change in the app repo, push to main
#    (edit index.html / app source), git commit, git push

# 2. GitHub Actions tab: build-and-update-config runs green
#    - builds image:SHA, pushes to ghcr
#    - commits "deploy: <service> <sha>" to homelab-cicd-config

# 3. config repo: confirm the bot commit bumped newTag

# 4. ArgoCD detects change (~3 min poll; force with `argocd app sync <service>`)
kubectl get application <service> -n argocd      # Synced / Healthy
kubectl get pods -n <service> -o wide            # new pod, on deus
kubectl rollout status deployment/<service> -n <service>

docs.title: Prove the GitOps guarantee (self-heal)
docs.text:
kubectl scale deployment/<service> -n <service> --replicas=3
# within ~1 min ArgoCD reverts to replicas=1 (the git-declared value)
kubectl get deployment <service> -n <service>

docs.title: 9. New-service checklist
docs.text:
For each new built-from-source service:

  • [ ] Create <service>-app repo with Dockerfile, source, .github/workflows/build.yaml.
  • [ ] Add CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN secret to the app repo.
  • [ ] Substitute <service>, <port>, <owner-lowercase> in workflow + manifests.
  • [ ] Add apps/<service>/ (deployment, service, kustomization) to homelab-cicd-config.
  • [ ] Push app repo → confirm Actions green → confirm bot commit in config repo.
  • [ ] Make ghcr package public (or add pull secret).
  • [ ] Apply the ArgoCD Application → confirm Synced/Healthy, pod Running.
  • [ ] (Optional) Add tunnel hostname + IngressRoute for external access.
  • [ ] Run the end-to-end test + self-heal proof.

For off-the-shelf images (no source build): skip the app repo and CI entirely. Just add apps/<service>/ to the config repo pointing at the public image, and apply the ArgoCD Application.

docs.title: 10. Common failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix repository name must be lowercase uppercase owner in image force lowercase with tr in workflow Build green but no deploy ArgoCD Application not created, or images: name mismatch (case) create Application; align name: exactly, lowercase Checkout config repo fails wrong repo name or missing/expired PAT fix repository:; regenerate CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull package is private make public or add image pull secret ArgoCD Unknown / repo error private config repo, no creds argocd repo add with read PAT Browser HSTS / self-signed error on .dev not going through the tunnel (stale hosts entry, DNS-only record) remove hosts entry; ensure proxied CNAME; verify edge cert with curl -sv ... | grep issuer Redirect loop behind tunnel app serves its own HTTPS run app in insecure/HTTP mode Tag never updates kustomize edit set image name mismatch name: in kustomization must exactly match built image (case-sensitive)

docs.title: Dockerfile Reference Guide
docs.text: A practical reference for writing Dockerfiles across common use cases. The goal throughout is the same: produce a small, reproducible, cache-friendly image, whether you're building for a CI pipeline, a registry push, or a Kubernetes cluster.

docs.title: 1. How a Dockerfile actually works (the mental model)
docs.text:
A Dockerfile is a sequence of instructions. Each instruction that changes the filesystem creates a layer — an immutable diff stacked on the previous one. The final image is all layers stacked together.

Two consequences drive almost every best practice:

  • Layers are cached. On rebuild, Docker reuses a cached layer if the instruction and all instructions before it are unchanged. The moment one instruction's inputs change, that layer and everything after it rebuild. This is why instruction ordering matters so much: put rarely-changing things (dependency installs) before frequently-changing things (your source code).
  • Layers only add, never subtract. Deleting a file in a later layer doesn't shrink the image — the bytes still exist in the earlier layer. To actually remove something, it must be cleaned up within the same instruction that created it (or avoided via multi-stage builds).

A build runs in a temporary container per instruction; the result is committed as a layer, the container is discarded, and the next instruction starts from that layer.

docs.title: FROM — the base image
docs.text:
Starts every build (or every stage of a multi-stage build). Defines the starting filesystem and OS userland.

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
FROM golang:1.23 AS builder        # named stage, for multi-stage
FROM scratch                       # empty — literally nothing
  • Pin a specific tag, never bare latest. nginx:1.27-alpine is reproducible; nginx silently changes under you and breaks any "exact build" guarantee your pipeline depends on.
  • For maximum reproducibility, pin by digest: FROM nginx:1.27-alpine@sha256:....
  • -alpine, -slim, and scratch variants are progressively smaller. More on base-image choice in §5.

docs.title: RUN — execute a command at build time
docs.text:
Runs a shell command and commits the result as a layer. This is where you install packages, compile code, create directories.

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Two forms:

  • Shell form: RUN apt-get update — runs via /bin/sh -c. Supports &&, pipes, variable expansion.
  • Exec form: RUN ["executable", "arg1", "arg2"] — no shell, no &&. Rare for RUN; common for CMD/ENTRYPOINT.

Chain related commands with && and clean up in the same RUN (see §3), since a separate RUN rm ... can't shrink the earlier layer.

docs.title: COPY — copy files from build context into the image
docs.text:
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
COPY go.mod go.sum ./          # copy just deps first (cache trick, §4)
COPY . .                       # copy everything
  • The build context is the directory you pass to docker build (usually .). COPY can only see files inside it — you can't COPY /etc/passwd.
  • Prefer COPY over ADD for plain files. COPY does exactly one thing.

docs.title: ADD — copy, but with extra magic
docs.text:
ADD does what COPY does, plus: auto-extracts local tarballs, and can fetch URLs. The magic is usually a footgun.

ADD project.tar.gz /app/       # auto-extracts the tarball
  • Use ADD only when you specifically want tarball auto-extraction.
  • For remote files, prefer RUN curl/wget (explicit, lets you verify checksums and clean up in one layer). Don't use ADD <url>.

docs.title: WORKDIR — set the working directory
docs.text:
WORKDIR /app

Sets the cwd for subsequent RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY, ADD. Creates the directory if absent. Use it instead of RUN cd /app — cd in a RUN doesn't persist to the next instruction (each RUN is a fresh shell).

docs.title: ENV — set environment variables
docs.text:
ENV APP_PORT=8080 \
    LOG_LEVEL=info

Persists into the running container (visible to your process). Use for runtime config defaults. For build-time-only values, prefer ARG.

docs.title: ARG — build-time variables
docs.text:
ARG GO_VERSION=1.23
FROM golang:${GO_VERSION}

ARG BUILD_ID                   # passed via --build-arg BUILD_ID=...
RUN echo "building $BUILD_ID"
  • Only exists during the build; not present in the running container.
  • An ARG before the first FROM is special — it can parameterize the base image, but is out of scope for stages unless re-declared.
  • Don't pass secrets via ARG — they're visible in image history. Use RUN --mount=type=secret instead (§6).

docs.title: EXPOSE — document the listening port
docs.text:
EXPOSE 80

Pure documentation/metadata. It does not publish the port — that's -p at run time, or a Kubernetes Service. Worth including so the image is self-describing (and whoever wires up ingress knows the port).

docs.title: CMD — default command
docs.text:
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

The default process the container runs. Overridable at run time (docker run image <other-command>). Prefer exec form (JSON array) so your process is PID 1 and receives signals (clean SIGTERM shutdown — matters for Kubernetes pod termination). Shell form (CMD nginx -g ...) wraps your process in /bin/sh, which swallows signals.

docs.title: ENTRYPOINT — the fixed executable
docs.text:
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/server"]
CMD ["serve"]                  # default args, appended to ENTRYPOINT

ENTRYPOINT sets the executable that always runs; CMD provides default arguments to it. docker run image migrate would run /app/server migrate. This ENTRYPOINT + CMD pairing is the idiomatic pattern for a single binary that exposes multiple subcommands (e.g. a server with serve / migrate / health verbs).

docs.title: The rest, briefly
docs.text:
• USER — drop to a non-root user. USER 1000 or USER appuser. Do this for anything you expose; running as root in-container is a needless risk.
  • VOLUME — declares a mount point for external data. In Kubernetes you manage this via PVCs instead, so you rarely need VOLUME in cluster images.
  • HEALTHCHECK — a command Docker runs to test liveness. In Kubernetes the kubelet's liveness/readiness probes supersede this, so it's often omitted for cluster workloads.
  • LABEL — metadata key/values. Useful for org.opencontainers.image.source so a registry (e.g. ghcr.io) links the package back to its source repo.
  • SHELL — change the shell used by shell-form RUN (e.g. to bash). Rarely needed.
  • ONBUILD — defers an instruction to child images. Niche; mostly avoid.
  • STOPSIGNAL — overrides the signal sent to stop the container. Rarely needed.

docs.title: 3. The cleanup rule (why images bloat)
docs.text:
Because layers only add, you must clean up inside the same RUN:

# GOOD — apt cache removed in the same layer it was created
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# BAD — the cache bytes are already committed to an earlier layer;
# this rm shrinks nothing.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Same logic for: pip install --no-cache-dir, npm ci && npm cache clean --force, go build caches, downloaded tarballs you extracted then deleted. --no-install-recommends (apt) avoids pulling optional extras you don't need.

docs.title: 4. Layer caching: order for fast rebuilds
docs.text:
The single highest-leverage technique. Copy and install dependencies before source code, because deps change rarely and source changes every commit:

# Node example
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./   # changes rarely
RUN npm ci                               # cached unless lockfile changes
COPY . .                                 # changes every push
RUN npm run build

# Go example
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./                     # changes rarely
RUN go mod download                       # cached unless go.mod/sum change
COPY . .                                  # changes every push
RUN go build -o /app/server ./cmd/server

If you wrote COPY . . before the dependency install, every one-character source edit would invalidate the install layer and re-download all dependencies — turning a 5-second rebuild into minutes. On a CI runner that's build minutes and queue time billed directly.

docs.title: 5. Choosing a base image
docs.text:
Base Size When Full distro (debian, ubuntu, golang) Large (100s of MB) Build stages; when you need a full toolchain -slim (python:3.12-slim, debian:slim) Medium Runtime when you need glibc + a package manager but not the full distro -alpine (nginx:1.27-alpine) Small (~5–50 MB) Runtime; musl libc. Watch for musl-vs-glibc quirks with some binaries/wheels gcr.io/distroless/* Small, no shell Runtime for compiled binaries; minimal attack surface, no shell to exec into scratch Empty Fully static binaries (typical static Go); nothing but your binary

Trade-off: smaller bases pull faster (shorter ImagePullBackOff window on Kubernetes), have fewer CVEs, but give you less to debug with (no shell in scratch/distroless). For a static Go service, scratch or distroless/static is ideal. For nginx serving static files, nginx:1.27-alpine is the standard.

docs.title: 6. Multi-stage builds (the big one)
docs.text: Build in a fat image with the full toolchain; ship only the artifact in a tiny image. This is the most important pattern for compiled languages.

docs.title: Go service → tiny final image
docs.text:
# ---- build stage: has the Go toolchain ----
FROM golang:1.23 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
# CGO_ENABLED=0 makes a fully static binary that runs on scratch
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -o /out/server ./cmd/server

# ---- final stage: just the binary ----
FROM scratch
COPY --from=builder /out/server /server
# bring CA certs if the binary makes outbound HTTPS calls
COPY --from=builder /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
CMD ["serve"]

The golang:1.23 toolchain (hundreds of MB) never ships. The final image is your binary plus certs — often under 20 MB. COPY --from=builder is the key: it pulls a file out of an earlier stage into the final one.

docs.title: Node app → built assets only
docs.text:
FROM node:22-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build              # produces ./dist

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

A static-site generator (Hugo, Astro, plain webpack/Vite) fits this exactly: a build stage runs the generator, the final stage is nginx serving the output.

docs.title: Python app → slim runtime
docs.text:
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
COPY . /app
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "-m", "myapp"]

docs.title: Static site (nginx serving files)
docs.text:
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
# custom nginx config if you need routing/headers:
# COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

daemon off; is required — nginx daemonizes by default, which would make PID 1 exit and kill the container. This keeps it in the foreground.

docs.title: Go binary with subcommands
docs.text:
Use the multi-stage Go pattern in §6. The ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] + CMD ["serve"] shape means:

  • default run → /server serve
  • a one-off Job that overrides CMD with ["migrate"] → /server migrate

This maps cleanly onto any single binary that exposes multiple verbs (serve / migrate / health), which is a common shape for a service that ships its own admin commands.

docs.title: A compiled tool that needs a shell for debugging
docs.text:
If scratch is too austere (you want to kubectl exec in and poke around), use distroless with a debug variant, or alpine:

FROM golang:1.23 AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates
COPY --from=builder /out/app /usr/local/bin/app
USER 1000
ENTRYPOINT ["app"]

alpine gives you a shell and apk while staying small — a good default while you're still iterating on and debugging a service, before you tighten it down to scratch/distroless for production.

docs.title: 8. Security and correctness checklist
docs.text:
• Run as non-root. Add USER once the process doesn't need root. Create a user in the build if needed: RUN adduser -D -u 1000 app then USER app.
  • Pin base image tags (and ideally digests) — reproducibility.
  • Don't bake secrets in. Not via ENV, not via ARG, not COPY .env. They persist in image layers/history. Use Kubernetes Secrets at runtime, or BuildKit secret mounts at build time: dockerfile RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci
  • Use a .dockerignore. Keeps junk (.git, node_modules, *.md, local env files) out of the build context — faster builds, smaller context, no accidental secret leakage: .git node_modules *.log .env
  • Exec form for CMD/ENTRYPOINT so signals reach your process (clean pod termination on Kubernetes).
  • Minimal final image — fewer packages, fewer CVEs, faster pulls.

docs.title: 9. Quick reference table
docs.text: Instruction Purpose Key gotcha FROM Base image / start a stage Pin the tag; never bare latest RUN Execute at build time → new layer Clean up in the same RUN COPY Copy context files in Source must be inside build context ADD Copy + tar-extract / URL fetch Avoid unless you want tar extraction WORKDIR Set cwd Use instead of RUN cd (cd doesn't persist) ENV Runtime env var Persists into the container ARG Build-time var Not in the running container; not for secrets EXPOSE Document a port Doesn't publish anything CMD Default command/args Exec form for signals; overridable ENTRYPOINT Fixed executable Pair with CMD for default args USER Drop privileges Set before the process runs LABEL Metadata image.source links registry package to repo HEALTHCHECK Liveness probe K8s probes usually supersede VOLUME External mount point Use PVCs in K8s instead

docs.title: 10. How a Dockerfile fits a build pipeline
docs.text:
A typical CI step builds from the repo root: docker build -t $IMAGE:$SHA -t $IMAGE:latest .. So the Dockerfile lives at the repo root, sees that directory as its build context, and should:

  1. Pin its base image — the image content becomes as reproducible as the SHA tag, so a given commit always produces a functionally identical image.
  2. Order deps-before-source so runner build minutes stay low.
  3. Multi-stage down to a small final image so ImagePullBackOff windows are short and the pull onto each node is quick.
  4. Add LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> so the registry package auto-links back to the source repo.

Off-the-shelf images (databases, Grafana, media servers, etc.) have no Dockerfile at all — they skip the build step entirely and are referenced directly by their upstream image tag in your deployment manifests.

docs.title: Dynamic Dev Container — Setup Guide
docs.text:
A disposable, cluster-scheduled VS Code dev environment that lands on whichever always-on node has capacity, deployed through the same git push → ghcr → ArgoCD pipeline as everything else. Doubles as a contained sandbox for letting an AI agent run without reaching the host or your LAN.

Two goals, one design. The disposability that makes this a clean platform-engineering pattern (stateless, scheduled, reproducible) is the same disposability that makes it a safe AI sandbox (blast radius resets to last git push; the network policy keeps the agent off your home network).

docs.title: 1. How it works
docs.text:
local VS Code (Remote-Tunnels extension)
        │  attaches to the named tunnel "homelab-dev"
        ▼
   Microsoft tunnel relay  ◀── code tunnel (in the pod) phones out on 443
        ▲
        │  pod scheduled by K3s onto deus OR nebula (prefers nebula)
   ┌────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  code-server pod                               │
   │   • init container: git clone → emptyDir       │
   │   • workspace = EPHEMERAL (resets on restart)  │
   │   • NetworkPolicy: DNS + cluster + internet,   │
   │     but LAN (192.168/16) BLOCKED               │
   │   • non-root, caps dropped, resource ceilings  │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

You connect to the cluster, not a host. The scheduler places the pod; your editor follows the tunnel, not an IP. That's the "dynamic" you asked for.

docs.title: Why code tunnel, not code-server (browser)
docs.text: You wanted your real laptop VS Code, not a browser tab. code tunnel runs Microsoft's tunnel host inside the pod; your desktop VS Code's Remote-Tunnels extension attaches to it by name. The pod can be anywhere — the relay handles reachability, so no ingress/IngressRoute is even needed for the editor itself.

docs.title: 2. The "dynamic placement" — what it does and doesn't do
docs.text:
Honest framing, because the word oversells easily:

  • Hard rule: the pod is schedulable only on deus or nebula, never legion (transient — it'd evict your editor when the GPU node sleeps).
  • Soft rule: prefer nebula (more RAM for compile/AI), fall back to deus.
  • Placement is decided once, at schedule time, from resources.requests + the preference. K3s does not rebalance a running pod. So "whichever is less loaded" means less loaded at the moment the pod is created, not a live load balancer. Restart the pod (delete it; the Deployment recreates it) to re-trigger placement.

This is the genuine, defensible version of dynamic — the same model real platform teams use. Live editor-session migration across nodes isn't a thing that exists cleanly; "stateless pod, reschedule freely" is the honest best.

docs.title: 3. Repos & files (mirrors your existing two-repo pattern)
docs.text:
code-server-app (new app repo — source + CI):

code-server-app/
├── Dockerfile               # toolchain baked in; runs `code tunnel` as non-root
├── entrypoint.sh            # clone workspace, start tunnel
└── .github/workflows/build.yaml   # same CI shape as nginx-app

homelab-cicd-config (existing config repo — add one folder):

apps/code-server/
├── namespace.yaml
├── pvc.yaml                 # tiny, tunnel-auth only (see §6 for the tradeoff)
├── networkpolicy.yaml       # egress containment
├── deployment.yaml          # affinity + hardening + ephemeral workspace
└── kustomization.yaml
argocd/
└── code-server.yaml         # the ArgoCD Application

docs.title: 4. Placeholders to substitute
docs.text:
Before pushing, replace these across the files:

Placeholder Where Value <owner> argocd app, deployment env, ci workflow your GitHub username (as-is) <owner-lowercase> kustomization, deployment image username lowercased <your-dev-repo> deployment.yaml (init + main REPO_URL) the repo you want to hack on in the sandbox node names deus/nebula deployment.yaml affinity confirm against kubectl get nodes

The lowercase rule is the same silent-failure trap from your nginx guide: kustomize edit set image is a case-sensitive string match. Mismatch = tag never updates, no error.

docs.title: 5. Standing it up (order matters)
docs.text:
# 1. Create the app repo on GitHub, push the Dockerfile + entrypoint + workflow.
#    Add CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN secret to it (reuse the same PAT as nginx-app —
#    it's already scoped to homelab-cicd-config).

# 2. Push apps/code-server/ + argocd/code-server.yaml to homelab-cicd-config.

# 3. First CI run builds the image. The dev image is BIG (Go+Rust+kubectl+
#    VS Code CLI) — expect the first build to take a few minutes.

# 4. Make the ghcr package public (simplest) OR add a pull secret:
#    GitHub → Packages → code-server-app → settings → Change visibility → Public

# 5. Register the ArgoCD Application:
kubectl apply -f argocd/code-server.yaml

# 6. Watch it land:
kubectl get application code-server -n argocd      # Synced / Healthy
kubectl get pods -n code-server -o wide            # note which node it landed on

docs.title: First-time tunnel login (one-time, see §6)
docs.text:
code tunnel needs to authenticate once. Read the device-login URL from the pod logs and complete it in a browser:

kubectl logs -n code-server deploy/code-server -f
# look for:  "To grant access ... open https://github.com/login/device
#             and use code XXXX-XXXX"

After login, the tunnel "homelab-dev" appears in your laptop VS Code: Command Palette → Remote-Tunnels: Connect to Tunnel → homelab-dev.

docs.title: 6. The one real wrinkle: ephemeral workspace vs. tunnel auth
docs.text:
The workspace is deliberately ephemeral (emptyDir): every pod restart re-clones from git, resetting the AI's blast radius. Good.

But code tunnel's auth token also lives in the container. If everything is ephemeral, every reschedule forces a fresh GitHub device-login. So the design persists only the tiny auth blob (a 64Mi PVC mounted at ~/.vscode-cli) while keeping the workspace ephemeral.

The catch: K3s local-path pins that PVC to one node. Once the pod creates the volume on (say) nebula, future reschedules stick to nebula — which partly defeats dynamic placement. Your three options, spelled out in pvc.yaml:

  • (A) Keep the PVC — first placement dynamic, then sticky; seamless reconnect. Default.
  • (B) Delete the PVC + volume/mount — fully stateless, placement dynamic on every restart, but re-login each cycle (one URL in the logs).
  • (C) Longhorn PVC later (NAS-gated) — node-independent replicated storage gives both persisted auth and free placement. The correct long-term answer.

If dynamic placement matters more to you than skipping the occasional re-login, start with (B) — it's the purest expression of the thesis. You can move to (A) or (C) anytime; it's a volume swap, not a redesign.

docs.title: 7. What's contained, and what isn't (the sandbox honesty section)
docs.text:
The NetworkPolicy (networkpolicy.yaml) enforces, via kube-router on your stock K3s:

  • ✅ LAN blocked — the agent cannot reach 192.168.x.x: not your router, not deus/nebula/legion management, not NAS admin, not other devices. This is the containment that matters most.
  • ✅ Link-local / metadata (169.254/16) blocked.
  • ✅ DNS + intra-cluster allowed (needed to function).
  • ⚠️ General internet on 443/80 is allowed — required because code tunnel and git clone need out. This is IP-based, so it's "all internet on 443," not a domain allowlist.

Plus pod hardening: non-root (uid 1000), all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, no host mounts, RuntimeDefault seccomp, and a hard memory ceiling so a runaway process can't OOM the node.

What this does NOT give you: a domain allowlist like your bash sandbox (github.com yes, everything else no). NetworkPolicy can't express that — domains map to rotating CDN IPs. That's the next section.

docs.title: 8. Follow-up: true domain allowlist via egress proxy
docs.text:
When you want the bash-sandbox-grade "only these domains" containment, it's a distinct project worth its own write-up:

  1. Run a small Squid (or similar) in-cluster with a domain allowlist (github.com, ghcr.io, pypi.org, crates.io, go.dev, the VS Code tunnel domains, …).
  2. Set HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY env in the dev pod to point at it.
  3. Tighten this NetworkPolicy to block direct 443/80 and allow egress only to the proxy's ClusterIP — so the proxy is the single way out and the allowlist is enforced.

That inverts the model from "block the bad" (LAN) to "allow only the good" (domains) — the real equivalent of your bash setup, and a legitimate platform concern (egress filtering) for the portfolio. Deliberately deferred so standing up the editor and enforcing domain policy don't tangle into one hard step.

One gotcha to expect when you do this: code tunnel's relay endpoints must be on the allowlist or the editor won't connect. Capture them from the pod logs during a working session before locking egress down.

docs.title: 9. Verify the containment actually works
docs.text:
After it's running, prove the LAN block bites (this is the satisfying part):

# should SUCCEED — internet is allowed
kubectl exec -n code-server deploy/code-server -- curl -sS -m 5 https://github.com -o /dev/null && echo "internet: OK"

# should FAIL/timeout — your LAN is blocked
kubectl exec -n code-server deploy/code-server -- curl -sS -m 5 http://192.168.1.250 -o /dev/null && echo "LAN: REACHABLE (BAD)" || echo "LAN: blocked (good)"

# should FAIL/timeout — router blocked
kubectl exec -n code-server deploy/code-server -- curl -sS -m 5 http://192.168.1.1 -o /dev/null && echo "router: REACHABLE (BAD)" || echo "router: blocked (good)"

If the LAN checks print "blocked (good)", the sandbox is doing its job.

docs.title: 10. Success criteria
docs.text:
• [ ] git push to code-server-app → new image in ghcr → ArgoCD syncs, no manual kubectl.
  • [ ] Pod schedules on nebula (or deus if nebula is loaded), never legion.
  • [ ] Laptop VS Code connects to the homelab-dev tunnel and opens the cloned workspace.
  • [ ] LAN-block verification (§9) passes.
  • [ ] Deleting the pod reschedules it (placement re-evaluated) and — with option A — it reconnects without re-login.

docs.title: 11. Where this sits in the project
docs.text:
This is your second app through the pipeline (the "prove the pattern generalizes" next-pickup from Phase 3), and the first one that exercises NetworkPolicy, pod security context, and scheduler affinity together — all directly transferable platform-engineering surface. It also unblocks the AI sandbox you wanted without a second piece of infrastructure: the cluster is the sandbox.

Natural follow-ups, in rough order: 1. Option (B) or wait-for-Longhorn (C) on the workspace/auth storage question. 2. The egress-proxy domain allowlist (§8) — own write-up. 3. A second profile of this image (e.g. a GPU-tolerating variant pinned to legion for AI inference work) once you want the GTX in the loop. ```

docs.title: K3s / Kubernetes — Working Reference
docs.text:
A practical guide to Kubernetes, oriented around K3s. It's written from the seat of someone running a small heterogeneous cluster — one always-on control-plane node plus a couple of workers of differing capability — so where a real cluster made a concept concrete, I've kept that context in. Everything here is standard Kubernetes unless a section is explicitly flagged K3s-specific.

Throughout, I refer to my own three nodes by name where it helps: - the control-plane node — a small always-on mini PC; runs the K3s server and anything stateful-ish that must never move. - a GPU worker — a laptop-class node with a discrete GPU; transient, so I taint it. - a storage worker — a desktop with the disks; where storage-bound work lands.

Substitute your own node names freely.

docs.title: 0. K3s vs Kubernetes — settle it first
docs.text:
K3s is Kubernetes. It's a CNCF-certified conformant distribution, so every API object, every kubectl verb, every manifest you write works identically on upstream Kubernetes, EKS, GKE, or a 500-node cluster. What K3s changes is packaging and operations, not the API:

Concern Upstream k8s K3s Install kubeadm + many components one curl \| sh binary Datastore external etcd cluster SQLite (single server) or embedded etcd (HA) CNI (networking) you pick & install Flannel, bundled Ingress controller you install Traefik, bundled Storage class you install local-path, bundled (default) Service LB cloud provider Klipper / ServiceLB, bundled Binary footprint large ~70MB, runs on a Pi

Takeaway: describe it as "K3s, a conformant Kubernetes distribution" — it signals you understand the distinction. The skills transfer directly; there's no "just homelab" asterisk on them.

docs.title: 1. The mental model
docs.text:
Kubernetes is a reconciliation engine. You declare desired state (YAML manifests); controllers continuously work to make actual state match. You almost never tell it to do a thing — you tell it what should be true, and it figures out the actions. If you run GitOps on top (e.g. ArgoCD's selfHeal), that's the same principle one layer up: the GitOps controller reconciles Git → cluster, while the Kubernetes control plane reconciles manifests → running containers.

The flow when you kubectl apply a Deployment:

You ──apply──▶ API server ──writes──▶ datastore (SQLite/etcd on the control-plane node)
                    │
                    ▼ (controllers watch the datastore)
        Deployment controller: "I need 1 ReplicaSet"
        ReplicaSet controller: "I need 1 Pod"
        Scheduler:             "that Pod goes on... a worker"
                    │
                    ▼
        kubelet on that worker: "pulling image, starting container"

Nothing pushes to nodes. Every node's kubelet pulls its assigned work from the API server. It's a pull model end to end.

docs.title: 2. The object hierarchy (what actually runs your stuff)
docs.text:
From smallest to largest, the chain that turns a container image into a running thing:

  • Container — your image (registry/app:tag), running.
  • Pod — one or more containers sharing a network namespace + storage. The smallest schedulable unit. Pods are cattle: disposable, replaceable, get a new IP every time. You rarely create these directly.
  • ReplicaSet — keeps N identical Pods alive. You rarely touch these directly.
  • Deployment — manages ReplicaSets to give you rolling updates and rollbacks. This is what you write for stateless services (web servers, APIs, proxies).
  • StatefulSet — like a Deployment but Pods get stable identities and stable storage (pod-0, pod-1). For databases and anything where identity matters.
  • DaemonSet — one Pod on every node (or every matching node). Used for node-level agents: Prometheus node-exporter, log collectors, CNI, device plugins.
  • Job / CronJob — run-to-completion and scheduled tasks. Backups, batch, migrations.

Supporting objects:

  • Service — a stable virtual IP + DNS name fronting a set of Pods (Pods die; the Service endpoint doesn't). Three flavors in §6.
  • Namespace — a logical partition (argocd, monitoring, kube-system, one per app). Scopes names and lets you apply quotas/policies per tenant.
  • ConfigMap / Secret — config and credentials injected into Pods as env vars or mounted files. Secrets are base64, not encrypted at rest by default.
  • PersistentVolume (PV) / PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) — storage abstraction. A Pod asks for storage via a PVC; a StorageClass provisions a PV to satisfy it.
  • Ingress / IngressRoute — HTTP routing from outside into Services. With Traefik you get its IngressRoute CRD, a richer Traefik-specific version of the standard Ingress object.

docs.title: 3. kubectl — the commands you'll actually run
docs.text: kubectl is your single interface. The pattern is almost always kubectl <verb> <resource> [name] [flags].

docs.title: Inspection (90% of daily use)
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -o wide              # all nodes, IPs, k3s version, OS
kubectl get pods -A                    # -A = all namespaces (kube-system too)
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o wide       # which node each pod landed on
kubectl get all -n <ns>                # pods, services, deployments, etc. in one ns
kubectl get deployment,svc,pvc -n <ns>

kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>     # events, why it won't schedule, image pull errs
kubectl describe node <node>           # capacity, taints, what's scheduled there

kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns>             # stdout/stderr
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -f          # follow (tail -f)
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --previous  # logs from the crashed prior container

docs.title: Interacting with running Pods
docs.text:
kubectl exec -it <pod> -n <ns> -- sh   # shell inside a container
kubectl exec <pod> -n <ns> -- nginx -t          # one-off command
kubectl cp <pod>:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./out.conf -n <ns>

docs.title: Port-forwarding (a common gotcha)
docs.text:
kubectl port-forward -n <ns> svc/<svc> 8888:80

If you run this inside an SSH session to a node, localhost:8888 binds to that node's loopback, not your laptop. Two fixes:

ssh -L 8888:localhost:8888 <node>      # tunnel the port back to your laptop, OR
kubectl port-forward --address 0.0.0.0 -n <ns> svc/<svc> 8888:80  # then hit the node's LAN IP

The clean long-term fix: copy the kubeconfig (/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml on a K3s server) to your workstation, rewrite the server: field to the control-plane node's IP (https://<control-plane-ip>:6443), and run kubectl locally. Then localhost means your laptop and forwards Just Work.

docs.title: Applying & deleting
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml       # declarative — create or update to match file
kubectl apply -k apps/<svc>/           # apply a Kustomize directory
kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml
kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <ns>       # pod gets recreated by its ReplicaSet — a quick restart

Prefer apply (declarative) over create/edit (imperative). Everything in the cluster should be reproducible from source. The imperative commands are for debugging and learning, not for the running state — and if you run GitOps, a selfHeal controller will literally undo any imperative change you make to a managed resource, by design.

docs.title: Rollouts (Deployments)
docs.text:
kubectl rollout status deployment/<svc> -n <ns>
kubectl rollout history deployment/<svc> -n <ns>
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<svc> -n <ns>          # roll back one version
kubectl rollout restart deployment/<svc> -n <ns>       # restart all pods (re-pull, re-read config)

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
kubectl scale deployment/<svc> -n <ns> --replicas=3
# (a GitOps controller reverts this if the app is git-managed — the self-heal proof)

docs.title: Quality-of-life
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A -w                 # -w = watch, live updates
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp   # what just happened & why
kubectl api-resources                  # every object type + its short name & API group
kubectl explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers  # inline schema docs
alias k=kubectl                        # everyone does this

docs.title: 4. Anatomy of a manifest
docs.text:
Every object shares the same four top-level keys:

apiVersion: apps/v1     # which API group+version owns this kind
kind: Deployment        # the object type
metadata:
  name: web             # unique within namespace+kind
  namespace: web
spec:                   # DESIRED STATE — the only part you really design
  replicas: 1
  selector:             # how this Deployment finds "its" pods (must match template labels)
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:             # the Pod blueprint stamped out N times
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }   # ← selector matches THIS
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: <control-plane-node>   # placement constraint (see §5)
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: registry/web-app:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
# status:               # ACTUAL STATE — k8s writes this, you never do

The labels/selector coupling trips everyone up early: a Service finds Pods by label selector, a Deployment manages Pods by label selector. If labels and selectors don't match, you get a Service with no endpoints or a Deployment that manages nothing. They're the glue.

docs.title: 5. Scheduling — placement in a heterogeneous cluster
docs.text: This matters most when your nodes are not interchangeable — different CPUs, some with a GPU, some always-on and some transient. The scheduler decides placement once, at creation time, based on resources.requests (declared, not actual usage) — there's no automatic rebalancing afterward. You steer it with four tools.

docs.title: nodeSelector — simplest, exact-match
docs.text:
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: <control-plane-node>    # "only here"

Good for "this must run on the always-on node" — I pin the GitOps controller and any always-up service this way.

docs.title: Node labels — your own taxonomy
docs.text:
kubectl label node <storage-node> role=storage
kubectl label node <gpu-node> gpu=true
kubectl get nodes --show-labels

Then nodeSelector: { role: storage } is more meaningful than a hostname and survives a hardware swap.

docs.title: Affinity / anti-affinity — expressive rules
docs.text:
nodeSelector is hard AND-only. Affinity adds OR, preferences (soft), and pod-relative rules:

spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:   # hard requirement
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: gpu
                operator: In
                values: ["true"]
    podAntiAffinity:                                     # spread replicas across nodes
      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - weight: 100
          podAffinityTerm:
            labelSelector:
              matchLabels: { app: web }
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

docs.title: Taints & tolerations — the node says NO by default
docs.text:
A taint repels Pods unless they explicitly tolerate it. This is exactly the pattern for a transient node: taint it so stateful/general workloads stay off, and only the workloads that opt in land there.

# on a transient node:
kubectl taint node <gpu-node> transient=true:NoSchedule

# only a pod with this toleration can be placed there:
spec:
  tolerations:
    - key: transient
      operator: Equal
      value: "true"
      effect: NoSchedule

Effects: NoSchedule (won't place new), PreferNoSchedule (soft), NoExecute (also evicts running pods that don't tolerate — this is what drains a node).

The combined pattern for GPU routing: label the GPU node gpu=true, and taint it transient=true:NoSchedule. A GPU workload then needs both a nodeSelector/affinity for gpu=true (to be attracted) and a toleration for transient (to be permitted). Attraction + permission — you need both, and that's the bit people forget.

docs.title: Resource requests & limits — feed the scheduler real numbers
docs.text:
containers:
  - name: web
    resources:
      requests:           # scheduler reserves this; used for placement math
        cpu: 100m         # 100 millicores = 0.1 core
        memory: 128Mi
      limits:             # hard ceiling; CPU throttled, memory OOM-killed if exceeded
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 256Mi

Without requests, the scheduler assumes ~0 and can overpack a node. On modest nodes (say 16GB) this bites fast — set requests so placement reflects reality.

docs.title: 6. Networking — how traffic actually flows
docs.text:
Three Service types, each a different exposure level:

  • ClusterIP (default) — internal-only virtual IP. Reachable as <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local from any pod. Most services should be ClusterIP and get exposed via Ingress.
  • NodePort — opens a high port (30000–32767) on every node's IP. Crude; mostly a debugging/legacy step. Usually skipped.
  • LoadBalancer — asks for an external IP. In cloud, provisions a cloud LB; in K3s, the bundled ServiceLB (Klipper) fakes it using node IPs. MetalLB is the common bare-metal alternative — but if you front the cluster with a tunnel (below), you may not need LoadBalancer Services or MetalLB at all.

A tunnel-based ingress path (the one I run) avoids opening any router ports:

Internet ─▶ Cloudflare edge (TLS) ─▶ cloudflared tunnel ─▶ Traefik :80
            ─▶ IngressRoute (Host match) ─▶ ClusterIP Service ─▶ Pod

No router ports opened, no MetalLB, no LoadBalancer Services. cloudflared is a dumb pipe; Traefik is the routing brain. Every new external service = one DNS record + one IngressRoute. It's one of several valid patterns — a LoadBalancer + MetalLB + real Ingress is equally legitimate; the tunnel just trades a dependency on Cloudflare for not touching the router.

DNS inside the cluster: CoreDNS (in kube-system) gives every Service a name. Pattern: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. From a pod in the same namespace, just <service> works. This is how one service finds another (e.g. a reverse proxy finding its upstreams).

The CNI (Flannel in K3s): gives every Pod a routable IP on an overlay network so any pod can reach any pod across nodes without NAT. You rarely touch it; just know the pod network (10.42.0.0/16 by default in K3s) is separate from your LAN (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24).

docs.title: 7. Storage — PVCs, StorageClasses, and node-locality
docs.text:
The PVC/PV/StorageClass dance:

  • A StorageClass is a provisioner — a recipe for making volumes on demand.
  • A Pod declares a PVC ("I want 10Gi, ReadWriteOnce").
  • The StorageClass dynamically creates a PV to satisfy it; the PVC binds.
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data
  namespace: web
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: local-path        # K3s default, lives on the node's disk
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi

# in the pod spec:
    volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: data
    containers:
      - name: app
        volumeMounts:
          - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/app }

Access modes matter for a multi-node cluster: - ReadWriteOnce (RWO) — one node at a time. Fine for single-replica apps. - ReadWriteMany (RWX) — many nodes simultaneously. Needs a networked backend (NFS, or Longhorn with RWX). Required for anything that must be writable from pods on different nodes at once.

Two common classes: - local-path (bundled, default): writes to a directory on whatever node the pod lands on. Fast, zero-config, but the data is pinned to that node — if the pod reschedules elsewhere, the data doesn't follow. Fine for state that lives on an always-on node. Not fine for anything that might move. - Longhorn (or similar distributed block storage): replicated across nodes, survives node loss, supports RWX, gives you snapshots. The "real" answer for stateful workloads — at the cost of needing dedicated disks and some operational care.

This is the crux of a "durable data lives outside the disposable layer" discipline: K3s-native local-path is convenient but node-fragile, so irreplaceable data belongs on a proper storage tier (a NAS/ZFS box over the network, or replicated Longhorn) rather than on whatever node a pod happened to land on. It's often reasonable to keep a database outside the cluster entirely until you have real replicated storage in place.

docs.title: 8. Configuration & secrets
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: app-config, namespace: web }
data:
  UPSTREAM_HOST: "backend.web.svc.cluster.local"
  log_level: "info"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: { name: app-secret, namespace: web }
type: Opaque
stringData:                 # stringData = plaintext in, base64 stored
  api_token: "s3cr3t"

Inject into a pod:

    containers:
      - name: app
        envFrom:
          - configMapRef: { name: app-config }
        env:
          - name: API_TOKEN
            valueFrom:
              secretKeyRef: { name: app-secret, key: api_token }

Secrets are base64, not encrypted. Anyone with kubectl get secret -o yaml can decode them. That may be acceptable behind a private network, but the "real" answer — Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or external-secrets — lets you commit encrypted secrets to a config repo, which plain Secrets can't safely do. If you're doing GitOps, this is the piece that makes secrets fit the model instead of being a manual out-of-band step.

docs.title: 9. Health & self-healing — the probes
docs.text:
Kubernetes restarts and reroutes based on three probes you define per container:

    containers:
      - name: app
        livenessProbe:        # "is it alive?" fail ⇒ kill & restart the container
          httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 80 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:       # "ready for traffic?" fail ⇒ pull from Service endpoints
          httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 80 }
          periodSeconds: 5
        startupProbe:         # "still booting?" protects slow-starters from liveness
          httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 80 }
          failureThreshold: 30
          periodSeconds: 2

The distinction matters: a liveness failure restarts the pod; a readiness failure just stops sending it traffic (no restart). Misusing liveness for a slow-but-healthy app causes restart loops. Any service you write yourself should expose a /healthz (and ideally a separate /ready) so Kubernetes can manage it properly.

docs.title: 10. Helm & Kustomize
docs.text:
• Kustomize: patches/overlays plain YAML, no templating language. An images: block in a kustomization.yaml rewriting an image tag in place is pure Kustomize. Built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k). Good for "same manifests, small per-environment differences."
  • Helm: a package manager. A "chart" is a templated, parameterized bundle; you install it with --set overrides or a values.yaml. Good for consuming complex off-the-shelf software (e.g. kube-prometheus-stack).

Rule of thumb: Helm to install other people's complex software, Kustomize to manage your own manifests. A GitOps controller like ArgoCD natively understands both, so either can sit behind the loop.

helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm install kube-prom prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  -n monitoring --create-namespace
helm list -A                    # what's installed
helm get values kube-prom -n monitoring   # what settings are active
helm upgrade kube-prom prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring -f values.yaml

docs.title: 11. K3s-specific operations
docs.text:
Things that are K3s-particular rather than generic Kubernetes:

# the kubeconfig (copy this to your laptop, rewrite the server: field)
sudo cat /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml

# server (control plane) service
sudo systemctl status k3s
sudo journalctl -u k3s -f                 # control-plane logs

# agent service — on a worker
sudo systemctl status k3s-agent
sudo journalctl -u k3s-agent -f

# the join token (to add a node)
sudo cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token

# add an agent (run on the new node)
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_URL=https://<control-plane-ip>:6443 \
  K3S_TOKEN=<token> sh -

# K3s bundles its own containerd + crictl for low-level container debugging
sudo k3s crictl ps                        # running containers at the runtime level
sudo k3s crictl images

# clean uninstall (K3s ships the script)
/usr/local/bin/k3s-uninstall.sh           # on a server
/usr/local/bin/k3s-agent-uninstall.sh     # on an agent

Node lifecycle (the graceful way to power a node down):

kubectl cordon <node>        # mark unschedulable — no NEW pods, existing stay
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data  # evict pods, prep for shutdown
kubectl uncordon <node>      # back into rotation

drain before powering a node down reschedules evictable pods elsewhere first — the right move for any node you shut down regularly (a transient laptop worker, a node you patch and reboot). DaemonSets are excluded because they're node-bound by definition; hence --ignore-daemonsets.

Bundled-component note: because Traefik, ServiceLB, and local-path ship inside K3s, they're managed by manifests in /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/. K3s re-applies these on restart. To disable a bundled component (e.g. swap Traefik for something else), start k3s with --disable=traefik rather than deleting the manifest, which would just get recreated.

docs.title: 12. A debugging playbook (the 80% of incidents)
docs.text:
# Pod won't start — read the events FIRST, they almost always say why
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>      # look at the Events: section at the bottom
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp

Common states and what they mean:

State Meaning First move Pending scheduler can't place it describe pod → no node matches selector/taint, or insufficient resources ImagePullBackOff can't pull the image private registry needs a pull secret, or wrong image name/case CrashLoopBackOff container starts then dies repeatedly kubectl logs <pod> --previous to see the death ContainerCreating (stuck) volume won't mount / image still pulling describe pod for the mount or pull error Running but no traffic readiness probe failing or label/selector mismatch check kubectl get endpoints <svc> — empty means selector miss Terminating (stuck) finalizers or a wedged node describe, check node health 
# Service has no endpoints? The classic label/selector bug:
kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns>     # empty = Service selector doesn't match any Pod labels
kubectl get pods -n <ns> --show-labels  # compare to the Service's selector

# Is the whole control plane healthy?
kubectl get pods -n kube-system         # CoreDNS, Traefik, metrics-server all Running?

# What's eating resources? (needs metrics-server, bundled in K3s)
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -A

docs.title: 13. Common workload shapes
docs.text:
A few recurring patterns, in increasing order of scheduling complexity:

  • Stateless service: Deployment + ClusterIP Service + IngressRoute, pinned to a specific node if it must be always-on. The template for everything stateless — web servers, APIs, reverse proxies.
  • GPU workload: Deployment with nodeSelector/affinity for a gpu=true label + a toleration for whatever taint guards that node + a GPU resource request (nvidia.com/gpu: 1, once the NVIDIA device plugin DaemonSet is installed). The device plugin is the missing link that exposes the GPU to the scheduler — without it, nvidia.com/gpu requests never satisfy.
  • Stateful service (database, etc.): StatefulSet + a PVC on replicated storage (Longhorn/NFS), not local-path, so the data survives a reschedule. If you don't yet have replicated storage, it's often cleaner to run the database outside the cluster than to pin it fragilely to one node.
  • Node-level agent: DaemonSet — exporters, log shippers, device plugins.

docs.title: 14. Minimal end-to-end example to internalize the model
docs.text:
Deploy something from scratch, by hand, once — then never again (because you'll move to declarative manifests / GitOps). It cements what the automation is doing for you:

kubectl create namespace demo

kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx:alpine -n demo
kubectl expose deployment hello --port=80 -n demo          # makes a ClusterIP Service
kubectl get pods,svc -n demo -o wide                       # see where it landed
kubectl scale deployment/hello -n demo --replicas=3        # watch 3 pods appear
kubectl get pods -n demo -o wide -w                        # spread across nodes?

kubectl port-forward -n demo svc/hello 8080:80             # (mind the SSH-localhost gotcha, §3)
# curl localhost:8080 → nginx welcome page

kubectl delete namespace demo                              # tears down everything in it

Then realize a GitOps loop does all of this from a git push — declaratively, self-healing, with the image pinned to an exact build. Being able to do it by hand and having built the automation that makes doing it by hand unnecessary is the whole competency.

docs.title: Quick reference card
docs.text:
# context & cluster
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl config current-context

# the daily four
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -f
kubectl exec -it <pod> -n <ns> -- sh

# apply / rollout
kubectl apply -k apps/<svc>/
kubectl rollout status deployment/<svc> -n <ns>
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<svc> -n <ns>

# scheduling
kubectl label node <node> <key>=<val>
kubectl taint node <node> <key>=<val>:NoSchedule
kubectl cordon/drain/uncordon <node>

# debug
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns>
kubectl top nodes ; kubectl top pods -A

# k3s host-level (on the node)
sudo journalctl -u k3s -f               # server (control plane)
sudo journalctl -u k3s-agent -f         # agent (worker)
sudo k3s crictl ps

docs.title: Why I Built the Cluster: Motivation, Objectives, and the Alternatives I Weighed
docs.text: A foundational document. Written after the fact, but describing the reasoning as it stood when I decided to build.

docs.title: 1. The motivation
docs.text:
The honest starting point: I'm a CS student in Singapore interest in the domains of computer systems, networks and graphics. I am primarily gearing towards CDN, SRE, and platform-engineering roles, and those roles have a chicken-and-egg problem. They want people who've operated real infrastructure: GitOps, observability, distributed storage, ingress, networking. The problem is that you don't get to operate real infrastructure until someone hires you into a role that lets you. Coursework doesn't fill that gap, neither does a tidy GitHub repo full of toy projects that never ran anywhere.

Over my 2 years as an undergrad in NUS (National University of Singapore), I have come to realise that the programming in CS isnt exactly the barrier for your projects. In the age of AI and thousands of projects executed through coursework or hackathons, you will come to realise what ultimately matters is that your project actually ships out and remain reliable during its lifecycle.
