So here comes the question of how. To do that, we must first somewhat understand the development lifecycle of software, from gathering the requirements to deployment and the monitoring + maintenance that comes after.

┌──────┐ → ┌──────────────┐ → ┌─────────────┐ → ┌────────┐ → ┌─────────────┐
│ Idea │   │ Requirements │   │ Feasibility │   │ Design │   │ Planning    │
└──────┘   └──────────────┘   └─────────────┘   └────────┘   └─────────────┘

      ↓

┌─────────────┐ → ┌──────────┐ → ┌─────────┐ → ┌─────────────┐
│ Development │   │ Build/CI │   │ Testing │   │ Release     │
└─────────────┘   └──────────┘   └─────────┘   └─────────────┘

      ↓

┌────────────┐ → ┌────────────┐ → ┌─────────────┐ → ┌─────────────┐
│ Deployment │   │ Operations │   │ Maintenance │   │ Feedback    │
└────────────┘   └────────────┘   └─────────────┘   └─────────────┘
                                                              │
                                                              ▼
                                                    [Requirements]

End-of-Life:
[Maintenance] → [EOL Planning] → [Decommissioning] → [Retirement]

As a student, you will typically learn the steps from Ideation all the way to development and perhaps the steps heading towards deployment. But have though about how you will actually serve your products to your "customers"?

Suppose that you are making a website. Ask yourself these questions: - How is my website hosted? - How does the domain name actually send user traffic to the place that hosts the website? - How is the website backend server actually implemented on the physical device? Afterall, your server must exist as a physical computer - How do we actually reconcile bugs or even service failures during deployments? Or better yet, how do we anticipate and plan for such cases?

There are many questions not yet asked for the average student like me trying to build our own projects that ultimately ends up in the dumpster due to the lack of deployment infrastructure. Answering these questions won't happen in a single weekend, it takes significant amount of time to grasp the IT infrastructure that exists within our world.

So the cluster exists to manufacture the experience I can't otherwise get. It's a place to make production-grade mistakes on my own hardware, on my own time, where the blast radius is my weekend and not a company's SLA. Every hard thing I'd eventually be expected to know on the job, why a CRD sync fails, how to keep a database's backups honest, what happens when self-heal fights a manually-edited secret, I wanted to have already hit, understood, and fixed at least once.

There's a second motivation underneath the career one, which is that I actually enjoy this. The cluster is a standing invitation to learn GoLang, to hand-write a sync protocol, to understand networking from the packet up. The portfolio framing keeps me honest about scope and sequencing, but the reason I keep coming back to it on weekends is that it's genuinely interesting to build (This is very important for us to not just suddenly burn out and drop the project altogether).

Furthermore, it also provides a highly available infrastructure to actually experiment, and most importantly, deploy any projects that you make. This itself would perhaps give you a sort of understand and appreciation for the infrastructure that has been built from the ground-up to make our daily lives possible (and also to give us CS students a job). You will come to see how many people have contributed towards the effort, especially in the world of open source, the millions of unpaid contributor keep up the dependencies that we rely on

docs.title: 2. The objectives
docs.text:
Concretely, I wanted the cluster to demonstrate, and force me to learn the following, in roughly this order of priority:

  • Container orchestration in practice, not in theory. A real K3s cluster across heterogeneous nodes, with workloads that actually have to be scheduled, placed, and kept alive.
  • GitOps as the operating discipline. Git as the source of truth, ArgoCD reconciling the cluster to match, CI building and pushing images. The whole git push → build → deploy loop, with no manual kubectl in the critical path.
  • Observability that means something. Prometheus scraping real services, Grafana dashboards I actually read, an understanding of the RED method and how metrics feed autoscaling, not a default dashboard I imported and forgot.
  • Networking depth. Reverse proxies and ingress (Traefik), load balancing (MetalLB), secure external access without opening my router (Cloudflare Tunnel), and a high-throughput private path (WireGuard/Tailscale). Eventually hand-building an L4/L7 proxy and a custom binary protocol to understand what the off-the-shelf tools are doing.
  • Distributed storage. Longhorn for replicated block storage, ZFS for the NAS layer, and a clear rule about which owns what.
  • Real, self-hosted services running on all of it, a portfolio site, a media server (Jellyfin), a file-sync system (Seafile), and my own hand-written Obsidian sync (obsync).

The meta-objective sitting above all of these: be able to explain why every choice was made. A cluster I can't reason about is just a pile of YAML. The value, to me and to an interviewer, is in the decision log, not the uptime number.

docs.title: 3. The alternatives: different ways of acquiring compute
docs.text: Before committing to owned hardware I did genuinely consider the alternatives. "Build a homelab" was the answer, but it wasn't the only option, and the reasons the others lost are part of the justification.

docs.title: 3.1 Public cloud (AWS / GCP / Azure)
docs.text:
The obvious default. Spin up managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE), pay by the hour, never touch hardware. You might have even learnt this back in school, or played with it yourselves.

Why it's attractive: zero capital outlay, real production-grade networking and durability, the exact managed services I'd use at work, and instant scale.

Why it lost, for this goal:

  • Cost shape is exactly wrong for a learning cluster. A homelab is a steady, always-on, high-utilization workload, the single worst fit for on-demand cloud pricing, which charges a premium precisely so you can scale to zero. I never scale to zero; I'd be paying the elasticity premium for elasticity I don't use. (The full numbers are here, but the headline is that the AWS-equivalent of my cluster runs roughly US$11,000+/year, and my entire hardware build cost less than one month of that.)
  • The managed layer hides the learning. EKS is the thing I want to understand the guts of. If AWS runs the control plane, provisions the storage CSI, and manages the ingress, I've learned to consume a platform, not operate one. The whole point is to be the person who runs it.
  • The bill punishes experimentation. Leaving a GPU node running over a weekend because I forgot is a rounding error on my electricity bill and a genuinely painful line item on a cloud invoice. Owned hardware makes mistakes cheap, which is what a learning environment needs.

Cloud isn't wrong, it's the right tool for spiky, unpredictable, or scale-out-fast workloads, and I'd reach for it in a heartbeat for a startup's production traffic. It's just the wrong tool for sustained self-education on owned baseline load.

docs.title: 3.2 A single powerful server / one big box
docs.text:
Buy one capable machine, run everything on it (maybe with VMs to fake multi-node).

Why it lost: the entire point is distributed systems. Scheduling across nodes, replica placement, node failure domains, "which node has the GPU," draining a node for a reboot, none of which is real on a single box. VMs can simulate it, but they can't teach me what happens when a physical node overheats or a laptop's battery-removed worker drops off the network. Heterogeneity and genuine node independence are features here, not accidents.

docs.title: 3.3 Raspberry Pi / ARM SBC cluster
docs.text:
The classic homelab starter: a stack of cheap Pis.

Why it lost (for the main cluster):

  • Architecture friction. My whole pipeline builds linux/amd64 images to ghcr.io. Going ARM means multi-arch builds via docker buildx — a real, ongoing tax on every image, for no learning benefit relevant to my goals.
  • Underpowered for the real workloads. Postgres, Jellyfin transcoding, a monitoring stack, dev containers — these want CPU, RAM, and real I/O that a Pi struggles with. I'd spend my time fighting resource limits instead of learning platform patterns.

It is also worth noting that almost every single piece of software that you use or integrate has a compability with x86. The same cannot be guaranteed for ARM. That is the reason why the first iteration of the Snapdragon Windows laptops flopped rather badly in the market.

(Worth noting: I kept a Pi cluster on the table as a separate project for CS3210 parallel-computing coursework, OpenMP/MPI compiled from source, where the arch concern disappears entirely. Different tool, different job.)

docs.title: 3.4 Free-tier / student-credit cloud
docs.text:
Stretch AWS/GCP free tiers and student credits as far as they go.

Why it lost: credits run out, and they run out fastest on exactly the always-on compute a homelab needs. The moment the credits lapse I'm back to the cloud cost problem, except now my "learning environment" has a countdown timer on it. It's a way to try cloud, not to live in an always-on cluster.

docs.title: 3.5 VPS fleet (cheap providers)
docs.text:
Rent several cheap VPSes and cluster them.

Why it lost: it's a middle ground that gets the worst of both. Still a recurring bill (smaller, but forever), still someone else's virtualized hardware so I don't learn the physical/node layer, and networking between providers is its own headache. The one place a cheap VPS did earn a role was as a potential WireGuard relay, a single tiny box for NAT traversal, which is a narrow, well-scoped use, not a home for the cluster.

docs.title: 3.6 Owned hardware — the choice
docs.text:
What I actually did: three heterogeneous always-on x86 nodes (a Lenovo M910q control plane, an i7-6700K desktop with a GTX 1080 doubling as the NAS, and a battery-removed laptop worker with a GTX 1060).

Why it won:

  • The cost shape fits. Capital cost paid once, then only electricity, and at Singapore tariffs that's a small monthly number for an always-on learning rig.
  • Hardware availbility. These kind of used and custom hardware is rather easy to obtain at a reasonable price in singapore.
  • I own every layer. From the physical node and the OS up through K3s, storage, networking, and the apps, nothing is hidden behind a managed abstraction. That's the entire pedagogical value.
  • Mistakes are cheap, so I experiment freely. Freedom is worth every single penny.
  • It's a genuinely learning experience. "I ran a multi-node K3s platform with GitOps, distributed storage, observability, and custom networking on my own hardware for months" is a concrete valuable project, especially if you can genuinely reason about it.

docs.title: 4. The honest caveat
docs.text: Owning the hardware is the right call for this goal specifically, but it is not apples-to-apples with the cloud, and I want to be clear-eyed about that. AWS bundles redundancy, 25Gbit networking, managed durability, and the absence of me crawling behind a desk at 3am because a MoCA link is flapping or some sync error in ArgoCD preventing the deployment from being updated. I'm not paying the cloud premium because, for a learning cluster, I don't need any of what it buys, and needing to learn all of that myself is the feature. If this were production traffic with real users and an SLA, the calculus would flip. The cluster is the right answer to "how do I learn to operate infrastructure," not to "how should a business run its workloads." Those are different questions, and keeping them separate is itself part of what I set out to understand.

docs.title: The Initial Planning: Tradeoffs and the Choices I Made
docs.text:
Foundational document. Covers the decisions baked in at the planning stage, before and during the early build, and the reasoning for each.

The first document covered why a homelab and not the cloud. This one covers the decisions inside that choice: the hardware, the software stack, the architectural rules, and the sequencing. Almost every one of these was a tradeoff, and the tradeoff is the interesting part.

docs.title: 1. The hardware plan and how it evolved
The original sketch vs. what I built
docs.text:
The initial concept, captured in the original spec, was a fairly textbook homelab: one Lenovo Legion laptop as control plane + worker, plus three budget N100 mini-PCs as worker agents, on a S$1,000 budget over 3–6 months. Clean, symmetric, easy to reason about.

What I actually converged on is messier and better: three heterogeneous always-on nodes using hardware I largely already had or could get cheaply.

  • deus: Lenovo M910q (i7-6700T class, ~16GB). Always-on control plane. Small, low-power, quiet — ideal for the one node that must never go down.
  • nebula: i7-6700K desktop, 24GB, GTX 1080. Doubles as the ZFS NAS and the Docker Compose host (This thing only cost me S$270 and 6 hours of cleaning and troubleshooting).
  • legion: a laptop with a GTX 1060, battery removed so it runs 24/7 as a worker.

Why these names for the machine? Well no real reason, I just find the latin names more interesting and easier to remember.

docs.title: The tradeoffs in that shift
docs.text:
• Symmetric N100 fleet vs. heterogeneous existing hardware. Symmetric nodes are easier to reason about and cheaper to buy new. But heterogeneous hardware I already owned was free, more powerful, and serves as a better learning experience. Real clusters are heterogeneous; learning to place a GPU workload on the one node that has a GPU, or to keep replicas off the node that overheats, is a feature of an uneven cluster. I traded tidiness for realism and zero marginal cost.
  • The Singapore pricing reality. My early assumption that N100 mini-PCs were sub-S\$200 didn't survive contact with Singapore retail, where new 16GB/512GB units land closer to S$400, and the genuinely cheap path is refurbished enterprise USFF boxes (HP EliteDesk, Lenovo ThinkCentre) off Carousell. This is part of why leaning on hardware I already had won: the "cheap mini-PC fleet" wasn't as cheap as the spec implied.
  • N100 mini-PCs stayed on the table as additive nodes if a discount ever put them under ~S$200, specifically because they're linux/amd64 and wouldn't break my single-arch image pipeline (unlike ARM Pis). Compatibility drove that constraint.

docs.title: 2. The software stack — what I chose and what I passed on
docs.text:
The stack was chosen to mirror what these tools look like in a real platform team, while staying light enough to run on modest hardware.

Layer Choice The main alternative I passed on, and why Orchestration K3s Full kubeadm Kubernetes. Too heavy for this hardware, and K3s is real Kubernetes (same API) with the operational fat trimmed. Single binary, bundled Flannel/Traefik. GitOps ArgoCD Flux. both are fine; ArgoCD's UI makes the reconciliation loop visible, which matters when the goal is learning. Ingress Traefik nginx-ingress. Traefik ships with K3s and became my single routing brain. NGINX will be used as web servers instead Load balancer MetalLB Cloud LB. Doesn't exist on bare metal; MetalLB is the answer for LoadBalancer VIPs on a home cluster. Public access Cloudflare Tunnel Port-forwarding. My ISP router was locked at planning time; the tunnel dials outbound, sidestepping inbound ports entirely. Private/bulk access WireGuard + Tailscale Cloudflare Tunnel for everything. the tunnel hairpins through an edge PoP and is slow for bulk transfer. Storage (block) Longhorn Rook/Ceph. Far heavier operationally; Longhorn is right-sized for three nodes. Storage (bulk/NAS) ZFS Plain ext4/mdadm. ZFS gives snapshots, checksums, and mirror integrity the NAS role needs. Secrets Sealed Secrets Vault / External Secrets Operator, overkill until I need dynamic secrets, rotation, or audit logging. Observability kube-prometheus-stack Rolling my own Prometheus/Grafana. the Helm stack is the industry-standard bundle, they work together and I might as well just use as it is. Database CloudNativePG Bare Postgres in a Deployment, or Compose Postgres. CNPG gives an operator that owns failover, backups, and WAL archiving.

docs.title: Two stack tradeoffs worth expanding
docs.text:
• Sealed Secrets over Vault. Vault is what "real" shops use, so there was a pull toward it for the portfolio optics. But it's a heavyweight stateful service to run and back up, and I don't need dynamic secrets or rotation yet. Sealed Secrets fits GitOps natively, encrypted secrets committed straight to Git, only the in-cluster controller can decrypt. The tradeoff I accepted: I must back up the controller's private key outside the cluster and outside Git, because losing it makes every sealed secret unrecoverable. That single backup is the load- bearing discipline of the whole choice. I will definitely switch over to Vault once a significant number of services warrant its use

  • CNPG over a shared Postgres. I decided on one CNPG Cluster per application rather than a single shared instance. Shared is cheaper on resources; per-app is cleaner blast-radius isolation and matches how you'd actually run databases in production. For a learning cluster, the isolation and the realism won over the resource saving.

docs.title: 3. The architectural rules I locked in
docs.text: These are the principles that recur through every weekly log. They're the actual value of the planning, the rules that made later decisions fast.

docs.title: "NAS owns data, K3s owns services"
docs.text: The cleanest line I drew due to the nature of a heterogenous cluster. Durable bulk data lives on nebula's ZFS pool; services live in K3s. This is why Seafile runs on Docker Compose on nebula and not in the cluster, it's a deliberate, data-safety exception, kept out of K3s so it doesn't depend on cluster health. The tradeoff: a little inconsistency (not everything isin K3s) bought a lot of data safety and a clear mental model.

docs.title: "Cloudflare Tunnel = dumb pipe, Traefik = routing brain"
docs.text: All routing logic lives in Traefik IngressRoutes. Cloudflare and Tailscale are ingress pipes that feed Traefik; they carry no routing intelligence. This is what lets me have multiple ingress paths (public tunnel, private tailnet) without fragmenting routing across them. The corollary rule: a single routing brain per-app proxies (like nginx fronting an out-of-cluster stack) are allowed only if scoped to that stack, never promoted to a second general-purpose ingress.

docs.title: Longhorn cannot use ZFS (We should perhaps help with this implmentation)
docs.text: A hard technical constraint I learned the hard way: Longhorn needs a dedicated disk formatted ext4/XFS at a stable mount path with multipathd blacklisted. It cannot sit on a ZFS dataset. This shaped the whole storage-hardware plan, I couldn't just carve Longhorn space out of nebula's ZFS mirror (and ZFS can't shrink a vdev in place anyway, so clawing space back would mean breaking redundancy or a full backup-destroy-restore). The clean answer was buy/acquire dedicated disks, which is what I did.

docs.title: "2 replicas = meaningful redundancy"
docs.text: Longhorn below 2 replicas gives no node-independent redundancy. So the target is 2, and since deus overheats (no replicas there), the replica pair is nebula + legion. The tradeoff accepted: with exactly two targets I have zero placement slack, but two honest replicas beats three where one node is thermally compromised.

docs.title: The GitOps repo conventions
docs.text:
• Two repos, always. App source (+ CI) separate from config manifests. Single-repo would create an infinite loop, because CI writes the new image tag back to the config repo, which would re-trigger CI. Splitting them breaks the loop. This isn't a style preference; it's structural.
  • Pattern B (upstream Helm charts): just an argocd/<svc>.yaml Application, no apps/<svc>/ folder.
  • apps/<svc>/ only when I author manifests myself; multi-source Applications when a chart needs my own values + custom manifests.

docs.title: The IaC layering boundary
docs.text: Ansible owns below-K3s node state; ArgoCD owns in-cluster workloads; the two must not overlap. I chose Ansible over Terraform because my manual work is machine configuration (k3s install flags, systemd units, ZFS, sudoers, WoL), not API-driven provisioning, which is Terraform's job and which I mostly don't have. And I chose to write playbooks retroactively (the next time I rebuild a node) rather than stopping a working build to Ansible-ify it. Bandwidth was the tradeoff: perfect reproducibility now vs. forward progress now, and progress won.

docs.title: 4. Sequencing: the deliberate order of operations
docs.text:
Planning wasn't just what to build but when, and the ordering was a series of explicit tradeoffs about managing simultaneous novelty.

  • CI/CD before everything else. A working deploy loop is the foundation every later service rides on, so it came first, even before the storage that some services needed.
  • Longhorn deferred until dedicated disks existed. Rather than fake it on local-path (which pins pods to nodes) or bodge it onto ZFS (impossible), I pinned the few stateful workloads to nodes and waited until I had real disks. The tradeoff: temporary node-pinning ugliness vs. doing storage correctly once.
  • Portfolio site before obsync. Both need Go. But obsync also needs Postgres and a hand-written sync protocol, three new hard things at once. The portfolio site is Go + a few JSON endpoints: one new hard thing. Doing the simpler one first means I learn the deployment shape and the language with low stakes before layering on distributed-systems correctness. This is the clearest example of my core sequencing rule: don't stack multiple new problems in one step.
  • Guides written alongside the build, not after. Turning each hard-won setup into a reusable guide (CI/CD, Docker, K3s, observability) meant the next service was a checklist, not a re-derivation.

docs.title: 5. What I consciously left open
docs.text:
Good planning also means naming what you don't decide. Carried forward deliberately:

  • Control-plane HA: deus is a known single point of failure. I decided not to chase HA prematurely: two etcd servers is worse than one (no quorum), real HA needs three, so a future mini-PC becomes a worker to shrink blast radius first.
  • KEDA / autoscaling: gated behind Traefik metrics existing first.
  • Renovate: planned for dependency PRs, not yet stood up.

Leaving these explicitly open, with the reasoning attached, is itself a planning choice. It keeps the scope honest and stops me from forcing premature answers to questions the cluster isn't ready to settle.

docs.title: Cost, Value, and the Reality of Compute in Singapore
docs.text:
Foundational document. The money argument, what the cluster cost to build, what it costs to run, what it's worth, and how that sits against the actual state of compute in Singapore in 2026.

All figures are current as of July 2026 and, where they change quarterly (the electricity tariff especially), I've dated them so a future reader knows to re-check.

docs.title: 1. Capital cost: what it cost to build
docs.text: The defining feature of my build is that most of the hardware I already owned or acquired cheaply, so my marginal capital outlay was low. But to make the value argument honest, it's worth pricing what this cluster would cost someone building it from scratch in Singapore today.

docs.title: What I actually spent
docs.text:
I wouldn't say this is a cheap project to make. But honestly, I believe this is one of the cheaper hobbies that you can have, and you at least end up with actualy tangible compute power.

Item Notes Approx. cost deus M910q Lenovo Thinkcentre Mini-PC Bought online, i7-6700T + 16GB Ram $280 nebula Used custom gaming pc Bought from a seller in Carousell, came with i7-6700K, 24GB Ram and a GTX 1080 $270 legion Lenovo Legion gaming laptop Used to belong to Red Hat, sold off for free in their company marketplace $0 Longhorn NVMe drives (×3, 256GB) Free used, from company IT (pretty good quality) S$0 legion's WD Red SA500 500GB SATA NAS-rated, for the Longhorn partition ~S$103 ZFS NAS drives (nebula) 2× ~3.6TB in a mirror $400 Networking (switch, cables, MoCA) Omada switch, Cat6, MoCA over coax ~S200 Misc (thermal pads, USB sticks, etc.) ~S$30

The total cost is about S\$1283, not too bad at this day and age with ballooning memory and storage prices, and the single most important storage component (the Longhorn drives) was free.

docs.title: What it would cost to build fresh
docs.text:
If someone replicated this from nothing, at Singapore retail (July 2026):

Item Qty Unit (S$) Subtotal (S$) N100 mini-PC (16GB / 500GB, new) 3 ~400 1200 — or refurb USFF (EliteDesk / ThinkCentre, Carousell) 3 ~300 900 Managed switch (TP-Link SG108E class) 1 ~40 40 NAS-rated SSD / drives for storage — — ~600 Cables, USB sticks, surge strip, misc — — ~80 Total (new mini-PCs) ~S$1920 Total (refurb path) ~S$1620

So a from-scratch equivalent lands right around the original S$1,000 budget under it on the refurb path. That's the capital number to hold in your head: a complete, capable multi-node K3s platform for roughly one thousand Singapore dollars, once.

docs.title: 2. Running cost: electricity is the only recurring line
docs.text: Once built, the cluster's only ongoing cost is power. And Singapore's electricity price matters a lot here, because it's currently at a record high.

docs.title: The tariff (dated, re-check quarterly)
docs.text: For 1 July – 30 September 2026, SP Group's regulated household tariff is 31.91 cents/kWh before GST, or 34.78 cents/kWh with 9% GST — the highest in Singapore's history, up 17% from the previous quarter, driven by higher natural gas costs. It's reviewed every quarter, and EMA has flagged Q4 could ease or rise further depending on global fuel prices. For this analysis I use the all-in S$0.348/kWh.

docs.title: The draw
docs.text:
The recurring cost is the always-on draw. All three nodes now run 24/7:

  • deus (M910q): idles low, ~15W.
  • nebula (i7-6700K + GTX 1080): the heavy one; higher idle ~50W, more under load.
  • legion (laptop, battery removed): modest, ~16W.

Realistic always-on total: ~80W idle, ~130W with moderate workload. Do note that the high idle is due to overhead power consumption. The overhead is due to motherboard and other components (GPU is your worst nightware here), not the CPU (especially the case with nebula, with only 5W CPU idle).

docs.title: The monthly bill
docs.text:
• At idle (~80W): 80W × 24h × 30d = 57.6 kWh → ~S$20/month
  • With moderate load (~130W): ~94 kWh → ~S$33/month

So realistically S$25–33/month, call it ~S$300–400/year. deus alone is almost free (~S$4/month); nebula with the 1080 is the main contributor.

docs.title: The one lever
docs.text: The GPU-heavy draw on nebula is the part of the bill that moves. When the GPUs aren't working, that wattage is waste. Historically I had cluster-shutdown.sh / cluster-powerup.sh + WoL to spin heavy nodes down, though now that legion and nebula are deliberately always-on for storage-replica and NAS reasons, I've traded some of that saving for availability. That's a conscious tradeoff: a few dollars a month for a cluster that's actually up when I want to build on it.

docs.title: 3. Value: what the cluster is worth
docs.text: Here's where the numbers become lopsided in the cluster's favour.

docs.title: The cloud-equivalent bill
docs.text:
Mapping my nodes to the nearest AWS instances (a GPU-worker-heavy cluster like mine maps to g4dn.xlarge-class GPU instances plus a t3.xlarge-class control node, with EBS gp3 for storage):

  • On-demand, this lands around US\$970/month ≈ US$11,600/year.
  • On 1-year reserved pricing it drops to roughly US$7,000/year.
  • And that's before the Singapore-region premium: ap-southeast-1 runs meaningfully higher than the us-east-1 reference (a g4dn.xlarge is ~US$0.526/hr in us-east-1; Singapore is higher still), so the real local figure is worse, not better.

docs.title: The comparison that matters
docs.text:
• Capital: my whole build (or a ~S$1,000 from-scratch equivalent) costs less than a single month of the AWS-equivalent on-demand bill.
  • Running: ~S\$20–33/month of electricity vs. ~US$970/month of cloud compute. The homelab's entire annual running cost is roughly what the cloud equivalent bills in a week and a half.
  • Over a year: owned hardware total (build + power) sits around S\$1,300–1,400 all-in; the cloud equivalent is US$7,000–11,600+. Roughly an order of magnitude difference.

docs.title: But value isn't only the dollar delta
docs.text:
The cloud bill buys things my cluster doesn't have, genuine redundancy, 25Gbit networking, managed durability, and no 3am debugging of a flapping MoCA link. I'm not paying that premium because, for a learning cluster, I don't need any of it. So the real value has two parts:

  1. The compute-per-dollar, which is overwhelmingly in the homelab's favour for a steady always-on workload.
  2. The learning and portfolio value, which is the actual point. The cluster is a standing, defensible demonstration of platform engineering — every post-mortem, every open item, every "here's why this CRD sync failed and how I fixed it" is evidence I can operate and reason about infrastructure. That's worth more to my career goal than the dollar saving, and it's something no amount of cloud credit would have produced, because the cloud hides the exact layers I needed to learn.

Put bluntly: I spent ~S\$1,200 once plus pocket change monthly to build something that would cost ~US$11k/year to rent and that teaches me the thing I'm actually trying to learn. The economics are firmly on the side of building.

Another thing that I must preface is that building the cluster my way would have you touching the hardware and configuring very fragile components such as the BIOS and manually tuning the custom setup. If you're rather new to PC hardware, it is perhaps not very ideal to buy random custom PCs online.

docs.title: 4. The reality of compute in Singapore, 2026
docs.text: Zooming out from my cluster to the environment it sits in, a few things are true about acquiring compute in Singapore right now.

docs.title: Electricity is the structural constraint on any local compute
docs.text:
Singapore generates ~95% of its electricity from imported natural gas, so the tariff tracks global gas prices with a ~one-quarter lag. In 2026 that's meant a climb to a record 34.78 cents/kWh (with GST) for Q3 — a 17% single-quarter jump. For a hobbyist homelab this is a rounding error (S$25–33/month). But it's the reason Singapore is an expensive place to run always-on compute at scale, and it's a real input into why large-scale compute here leans toward efficiency and toward the cloud's shared-infrastructure model. Land and power are both scarce and priced accordingly. The lesson scales inversely: small always-on rigs are cheap to run; large ones are penalised by exactly the same tariff.

Fun fact: Despite being an island with no natural resources, the electricity prices here are still cheaper than the UK or Australia.

docs.title: The cloud is dominant here, and the pricing reflects premium demand
docs.text: Singapore is a major cloud hub — AWS (ap-southeast-1), GCP, and Azure all have strong regional presence, and ap-southeast-1 offers 800+ EC2 instance types. But regional pricing runs above the US reference regions. For businesses with spiky or unpredictable load, or that need managed durability and compliance, the cloud is the default and a sensible one. The Singapore premium is the price of low latency to a dense Southeast Asian market.

docs.title: The buy-vs-rent line: when local hardware wins
docs.text:
The principle that governs the whole comparison: cloud wins for spiky or unpredictable load; owned hardware wins for steady, high, predictable utilisation, because the cloud's core value is elasticity, and if you never scale to zero you're paying an elasticity premium for nothing. The signals that tip an organisation toward owning or colocating hardware:

  • Flat, high baseline utilisation (nodes pinned at 60–80% around the clock) — the classic "we're paying a 3–5× markup on compute we could own" realisation.
  • Sustained spend into the seven-figures-a-year range, where it earns a dedicated finance/infra analysis.
  • GPU-heavy workloads, where rental premiums accelerate the breakeven.
  • Heavy data egress, where cloud pricing punishes moving data out.
  • Regulatory or latency requirements that favour owned/colocated kit.

Real companies have made exactly this move at scale, Dropbox and 37signals/ Basecamp are the well-known cloud-repatriation cases. The honest counterweight is that owning hardware demands headcount and operational burden that erodes the savings, which is why the common landing spot is hybrid: own the steady baseline, burst into cloud for peaks.

docs.title: My cluster as a micro-version of that same logic
docs.text: My design is the hybrid principle in miniature. deus is the always-on baseline (cheap to keep up); heavy GPU draw is spun up only when needed; Cloudflare Tunnel (essentially free public ingress) handles the low-bandwidth public surface while owned WireGuard handles bulk transfer. I'm making the same steady-baseline-vs- elastic-burst tradeoffs a real infra team makes, just at a scale where the whole year's power bill is less than a fortnight of the cloud-equivalent invoice.

docs.title: 5. The bottom line
docs.text:
• Capital: ~S$1,200 once, more with further upgrades or additional nodes.
  • Running: ~S$25–33/month of electricity at the current record-high tariff the only recurring cost, and a small one.
  • Cloud-equivalent: ~US$7,000–11,600+/year, higher still at Singapore-region pricing.
  • Value: an order-of-magnitude compute-per-dollar advantage for this always-on workload, plus the learning and portfolio value that was the actual goal — which the cloud would have hidden rather than taught.

Money well spent. The hardware is already amortised many times over against the cloud line item, the electricity is the rounding error, and the thing I walk away with, the ability to operate and reason about a real platform, is exactly what I set out to buy.

You would perhaps argue the true resource being spent here is time. That is correct. But it is still time well spent learning the infrastructure in a practical manner, as well as a hobby worth exploring.

Tariff figure: SP Group regulated tariff, Q3 2026 (1 Jul–30 Sep), 34.78 ¢/kWh incl. GST — re-check quarterly. Cloud figures: AWS on-demand, us-east-1 reference with note that ap-southeast-1 runs higher; re-verify at aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing before quoting.

docs.title: Homelab Kubernetes Platform — Architecture
docs.text:
A three-node K3s cluster running GitOps-managed services, with a split public/tailnet ingress model and Longhorn distributed storage. This document captures the network topology (how traffic reaches the cluster) and the internal cluster topology (how workloads, storage, and GitOps fit together).

Domains: *.packetcraft.dev (public, via Cloudflare Tunnel) · *.lab.packetcraft.dev (tailnet-only) Source of truth: BarneyLaw/homelab-cicd-config (GitHub) → ArgoCD

docs.title: 1. Node inventory
docs.text:

docs.title: 2. Network topology
docs.text:
How the two ingress planes (public + private) reach a single Traefik routing brain.

flowchart TB
    subgraph internet["🌐 Internet"]
        user_pub["Public user<br/>*.packetcraft.dev"]
        user_priv["You / admin devices<br/>*.lab.packetcraft.dev"]
    end

    subgraph cf["Cloudflare Edge"]
        cf_tunnel["Cloudflare Tunnel<br/>(TLS terminated at edge)"]
        cf_dns_grey["Grey-cloud A records<br/>→ private 192.168.1.x IPs"]
    end

    subgraph tailnet["Tailscale Tailnet"]
        ts_router["Subnet router on deus<br/>advertises 192.168.1.0/24"]
    end

    wg["WireGuard<br/>UDP 51820<br/>(port-forwarded via Singtel ONR)<br/>high-throughput admin path"]

    subgraph lan["🏠 Home LAN — 192.168.1.0/24"]
        direction TB

        subgraph deus_node["deus · 192.168.1.250 (control plane)"]
            cloudflared["cloudflared<br/>(outbound-only, dumb pipe)"]
            traefik["Traefik<br/>★ single routing brain<br/>IngressRoutes"]
            metallb_vip["MetalLB VIP<br/>(Traefik LoadBalancer)"]
        end

        svc_pool["K3s Services / Pods<br/>(nebula · legion)"]
    end

    user_pub -->|"outbound-only<br/>connection"| cf_tunnel
    cf_tunnel -.->|"http://localhost:80"| cloudflared
    cloudflared --> traefik

    user_priv -->|"resolves to<br/>private IP"| cf_dns_grey
    cf_dns_grey -.->|"routed over"| ts_router
    ts_router --> metallb_vip
    wg --> metallb_vip
    metallb_vip --> traefik

    traefik -->|"Host-based routing"| svc_pool

    classDef edge fill:#f38020,stroke:#c25e0d,color:#fff
    classDef ts fill:#4b5563,stroke:#1f2937,color:#fff
    classDef brain fill:#2563eb,stroke:#1e40af,color:#fff
    classDef node fill:#e0e7ff,stroke:#6366f1,color:#111

    class cf_tunnel,cf_dns_grey edge
    class ts_router,wg ts
    class traefik brain
    class cloudflared,metallb_vip,svc_pool node

Two ingress pipes, one brain. Cloudflare Tunnel (public, outbound-only, no open ports) and Tailscale/WireGuard (private) are dumb pipes. All routing logic lives in Traefik IngressRoutes. This is the single-routing-brain principle: per-app proxies are scoped to their own stack and never become a second general-purpose ingress.

Access path Domain TLS Reaches Cloudflare Tunnel *.packetcraft.dev Cloudflare edge cert Public services Tailscale subnet router *.lab.packetcraft.dev Let's Encrypt wildcard (cert-manager DNS-01) Tailnet-only services WireGuard (UDP 51820) private IPs — High-throughput admin path

docs.title: 4. GitOps deployment flow
docs.text:
The git push → build → deploy loop that stands up every built-from-source service.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Dev as You (git push)
    participant App as app repo
    participant CI as GitHub Actions
    participant GHCR as ghcr.io
    participant Cfg as homelab-cicd-config
    participant Argo as ArgoCD
    participant K3s as K3s cluster

    Dev->>App: push to main
    App->>CI: trigger build.yaml
    CI->>GHCR: build + push image:SHA
    CI->>Cfg: kustomize edit set image → commit tag bump
    Note over CI,Cfg: fine-grained PAT (Contents: RW)<br/>CI has NO cluster access
    Argo->>Cfg: watch / detect new commit (~3 min poll)
    Argo->>K3s: reconcile Deployment to image:SHA
    K3s-->>Argo: Synced / Healthy
    Note over Argo,K3s: selfHeal reverts manual drift<br/>prune removes deleted resources

Two-repo split. CI writes to the config repo; ArgoCD reads from it. They never talk directly — a single repo would loop (CI's write-back re-triggers CI). Off-the-shelf images (Grafana, Jellyfin) skip CI entirely: just an apps/<svc>/ manifest + ArgoCD Application.

docs.title: 5. Key architectural principles
docs.text:
• NAS owns data, K3s owns services. Seafile lives on Compose for data-safety; ZFS tank on nebula holds durable state. Jellyfin placement remains open (GPU is on nebula, a Compose host).
  • Cloudflare Tunnel = dumb pipe, Traefik = routing brain. All routing logic in IngressRoutes; ingress pipes just feed it.
  • Single routing brain. Per-app proxies stay scoped to their stack — never a second general-purpose ingress.
  • Longhorn cannot use ZFS. Needs a dedicated disk formatted ext4/XFS at a stable mount, multipathd blacklisted. 2 replicas = the floor for node-independent redundancy.
  • selfHeal + Helm-managed secrets = churn. Chart-owned credentials get reset on reconcile → migrate to existingSecret + SealedSecret.
  • Sealed Secrets key backup is critical. Losing the controller private key makes all sealed secrets unrecoverable.
  • Ansible below K3s, ArgoCD in-cluster. The two layers must not overlap.

docs.title: Week 1: The Genesis, Physical Network and Getting the Layer-1 Right
docs.text:
Covers roughly 6–10 May 2026. Before this, there was no cluster, just a spec and a room with a coax outlet.

This is the true beginning. Before any OS, before K3s, before a single line of YAML, I had to solve a dumb but blocking physical problem: my room has no Ethernet port, only a coax outlet. Everything else in this entire project sits on top of the network I built in this first stretch, so it's worth writing down properly.

docs.title: 1. The problem: getting a wired LAN into a room with no Ethernet
docs.text: My room in the condo has a coax outlet but no RJ45. WiFi was a non-starter for a cluster: it adds latency, drops packets, and makes inter-node K3s communication unreliable. I needed real wired Ethernet to the nodes. The answer was MoCA (Multimedia over Coax): adapters that tunnel Ethernet over the existing coaxial wiring already in the walls.

docs.title: The coax splitter question
docs.text:
The first real snag was the house's existing coax splitter. It was rated only 5–1000 MHz, and MoCA 2.5 operates well above that (up into the ~2.6 GHz range). A splitter that cuts off at 1 GHz will simply kill the MoCA signal. So I planned to replace it with a MoCA-rated splitter (10 MHz–2.6 GHz): a single 1→6 unit with power-pass ports, good port-to-port isolation, and low insertion loss, compatible with MoCA 2.5/3.0.

The other physical-layer detail: a PoE filter (Point-of-Entry filter) between the router side and the coax input. This keeps the MoCA signal inside the house (reflecting it back rather than letting it leak out to the street / neighbours), which both improves signal quality and is good practice for security. Worth confirming you can swap a condo splitter yourself; in my case, yes.

docs.title: 2. The physical topology
docs.text:
Four cables, one clean chain. This is the layer-1 map the whole cluster runs on:

Router (main hall)
  │  Ethernet
MoCA adapter #1  ── coax ──▶  (wall coax wiring)
                                    │
                              MoCA adapter #2 (my room)
                                    │  Ethernet
                              Omada 8-port switch
                                 │        │        │
                              node       node     node

Concretely:

  1. At the router: Ethernet from a router LAN port into MoCA adapter #1; coax from adapter #1 into the wall outlet.
  2. In my room: coax from the wall outlet into MoCA adapter #2; Ethernet from adapter #2 into any port on the TP-Link Omada 8-port easy-smart switch.
  3. From the switch: one Ethernet run to each node.

The switch is a managed (easy-smart) unit deliberately: it gives me VLANs and QoS later for the "isolate cluster traffic" learning exercise, but I explicitly deferred all VLAN config. At this stage it's just a flat switch. Get layer-1 working first; segment it later.

docs.title: Verifying it worked
docs.text: Dead simple: once the MoCA adapters sync (1–2 minutes, watch the link LEDs), every node pulls a DHCP address and reaches the internet. ping 8.8.8.8 from each machine → physical network done. No software, no cleverness, just confirm the pipe carries packets.

docs.title: 3. The first hardware, and the control-plane decision
docs.text:
I started with two machines on hand:

  • A laptop: i7-8750H, 16GB, GTX 1060, 256GB SSD + HDD. (This becomes legion.)
  • A Lenovo M910q mini-PC: i7-6700T, 16GB, 256GB SSD. (This becomes deus.)

My initial instinct, straight from the spec, was to make the laptop the control plane since it's the beefier machine. I talked myself out of it, and this was the first genuinely important architectural call of the project:

The M910q is the better control plane. The reasoning:

  • The i7-6700T is a 35W enterprise part built for 24/7 operation. It idles at ~10–15W. The K3s server process is tiny (it barely touches CPU or RAM), so "beefier" is irrelevant for the control-plane role.
  • The laptop idles far higher (~40W+, more with the GPU) and carries real liabilities for an always-on box: lid-close sleep, aggressive power management, accidental shutdowns.
  • Power math (Singapore, ~S$0.30/kWh at the time): a 50W-idle machine costs ~S$130/year to leave running; the M910q at 15W costs ~S$40/year. For the one node that must never go down, low, boring, and always-on beats fast.

So the plan flipped: M910q = always-on control plane + worker; laptop = optional burst worker (powered on when I want the extra cores or the GPU). K3s handles nodes joining and leaving gracefully, so the cluster's core would be stable on low-power hardware even with the laptop coming and going, which is closer to how real infrastructure is built anyway (dedicated always-on control plane, not someone's daily-driver laptop).

(This laptop-is-transient framing held for weeks and shaped many decisions, until I later pulled its battery and made it permanently always-on. But at genesis, "laptop = comes and goes" was the working assumption.)

docs.title: 4. Why this matters
docs.text:
None of this is glamorous; it's coax splitters and ping tests. But it's the foundation literally everything else stands on, and two lessons from it recur through the whole project:

  • Solve the physical layer first, completely, before touching software. A flaky MoCA link or a wrong-spec splitter would have looked like a hundred different software bugs later. Getting layer-1 rock-solid up front saved me from chasing ghosts.
  • "Most powerful machine" is the wrong question for a role. The control plane wants reliability and low idle power, not raw horsepower. Matching hardware characteristics to the job (not the spec sheet) is a theme that comes back again and again (GPU placement, storage nodes, thermal-aware scheduling).

docs.title: State at the end of this stretch
docs.text:
• Physical wired LAN into the room via MoCA over coax, through an Omada switch.
  • Two machines identified and roles decided: M910q → control plane, laptop → burst worker.
  • No OS reinstalls or K3s yet; that's next.

docs.title: Open / next
docs.text:
• Install Ubuntu Server on both nodes, set static IPs, bring up K3s.
  • VLAN segmentation on the Omada switch (deferred).
  • A third, more powerful node and a dedicated NAS were already planned (the spec anticipated a Ryzen/desktop power node and a Carousell NAS tower).

docs.title: Week 2: OS, Static IPs, and Bringing the Cluster to Life
docs.text:
Covers roughly 10–14 May 2026. The physical network is done; now the nodes get an OS and K3s.

With the MoCA LAN solid, this stretch was about turning bare machines into a working K3s cluster: identical OS on every node, static IPs so nothing drifts, the K3s server/agent join, and the first node labels. By the end I had a real two-node cluster serving a test workload.

docs.title: 1. The OS choice: Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS on everything
docs.text:
I standardized on Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS, headless, SSH-only, on every node. The laptop had actually come to me running Fedora (it was ex-Red Hat hardware), and I deliberately wiped it to match. The reasoning is worth keeping, because "just use what's already on it" was tempting:

Homogeneity is worth more than convenience. When every node runs the same OS, every troubleshooting session, kernel tweak, and package install is identical across the cluster. Most K3s guides, Helm charts, and Stack Overflow answers assume Ubuntu/Debian. Fedora would have meant dnf vs apt, firewalld vs ufw, and SELinux enabled by default, which actively interferes with K3s networking if you don't configure it. One OS, one mental model. I traded a little setup effort for never having to think "wait, which node is this?" again.

Also settled here (before installing anything): K3s over MicroK8s. K3s is a single static binary from Rancher/SUSE: it strips cloud-provider cruft, uses SQLite by default (or embedded etcd for HA), bundles Flannel (CNI) and Traefik (ingress), and has a dead-simple one-curl server/agent join model. It's real conformant Kubernetes with the operational fat trimmed, exactly right for modest hardware.

docs.title: 2. The install pattern (repeated per node)
docs.text:
For each machine, the same sequence:

  1. BIOS first. Boot order to prioritize the OS SSD; enable AC power recovery / auto-power-on (so a node restarts itself after a power blip); disable sleep/hibernate where the option exists.
  2. A specific BIOS-menu gotcha I hit: the boot menu showed two SSDs, the USB installer, and an "EFI PXE Network" entry. Correct order: USB first (just to run the installer), then the OS SSD, then the other SSD, then PXE last; PXE is network-boot, unneeded, and only adds a boot delay if it's higher.
  3. In the installer's storage menu: the OS goes on the SSD (the install target under "used devices"); the secondary HDD sits in "available devices" untouched; partition and mount it later. Don't configure it during install.
  4. Ubuntu Server install, headless, no desktop. Critical screen: enable "Install OpenSSH server", that's the remote access the whole headless model depends on. Import GitHub SSH keys here if available. Skip all the featured server snaps (K3s comes later, by hand).
  5. Static IP via netplan. DHCP is fine for the first boot, but the nodes need stable addresses so the K3s join target never drifts. Find the interface with ip a / ip link (likely eno1 or enp0s31f6 on this hardware), then edit /etc/netplan/…yaml:

yaml network: version: 2 ethernets: eno1: # replace with the actual interface name dhcp4: no addresses: - 192.168.1.x/24 # a static IP outside the router's DHCP range routes: - to: default via: 192.168.1.1 nameservers: addresses: [1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8]

sudo netplan apply, verify with ip a, confirm internet with ping 1.1.1.1. 4. SSH in from my daily driver, then unplug monitor and keyboard; the node is now headless and remote-managed. 5. Housekeeping: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y, and sudo timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Singapore.

docs.title: 3. The laptop's extra steps
docs.text:
The laptop (soon legion) needed handling the others didn't, because at this stage it was still meant to be a come-and-go burst node:

  • Disable lid-close suspend: otherwise closing the lid kills the node. In /etc/systemd/logind.conf: HandleLidSwitch=ignore HandleLidSwitchExternalPower=ignore HandleLidSwitchDocked=ignore then sudo systemctl restart systemd-logind.
  • Disable the discrete GTX 1060. It just burns 5–20W idle if I'm not using it for GPU work. Either blacklist the modules (nouveau/nvidia in /etc/modprobe.d/, then update-initramfs -u), or (the cleaner route I took) envycontrol -s integrated. Reversible later when I actually want NVENC for Jellyfin.
  • On the battery question: at this point I decided not to remove it. The Legion's battery is internal (non-trivial to pull), modern charge controllers handle being plugged in fine, and the battery is a graceful-shutdown buffer against power flicker. (I reversed this much later, pulling it to make legion truly always-on, but at genesis, leave-it-in was the call.)

docs.title: 4. Bringing up K3s
docs.text:
The join model is as simple as advertised.

Server (on the M910q / deus):

curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -

This installs K3s with the control plane and worker enabled by default (no --disable-agent), which is what I want since deus is a permanent worker too. Then:

sudo kubectl get nodes                              # deus, Ready
sudo cat /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/node-token     # grab the join token

Agent (on the laptop / legion):

curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | K3S_URL=https://<deus-ip>:6443 K3S_TOKEN=<token> sh -

Verify from deus: kubectl get nodes shows both nodes Ready. Two-node cluster alive.

docs.title: 5. First node labels and a test workload
docs.text:
Immediately after the join, I labelled the nodes so scheduling intent was baked in from the start rather than bolted on later:

kubectl label node <deus>   node-type=always-on
kubectl label node <legion> node-type=on-demand
kubectl label node <legion> workload-type=stateless-only   # no stateful pods here

The stateless-only intent on legion follows directly from the "laptop comes and goes" assumption: no Longhorn replicas, no stateful workloads on a node that might leave. (The plan also anticipated laptop taints, node-role=on-demand:NoSchedule with tolerations only on burst workloads, using soft preferredDuringScheduling affinity for most workloads so the cluster stays flexible if a node drops.)

Then a throwaway test to confirm health:

kubectl create deployment test-nginx --image=nginx --replicas=2
kubectl expose deployment test-nginx --port=80 --type=NodePort
kubectl get pods -o wide     # one pod per node

Hitting the NodePort from another LAN device served the nginx welcome page → cluster genuinely works end to end.

docs.title: 6. Node identities (the names that stick)
docs.text:
The naming convention that runs through everything from here:

  • deus: M910q, control plane, 192.168.1.250.
  • legion: the laptop worker, 192.168.1.249.
  • nebula: the desktop/NAS node, 192.168.1.248 (acquired around now; brought fully online shortly after, see Week 0B).

Static IPs live in the 192.168.1.248–250 range (a small reserved block at the top of the subnet), well clear of the router's DHCP pool.

docs.title: State at the end of this stretch
docs.text:
• Ubuntu Server 24.04 on every node, homogeneous.
  • Static IPs via netplan; headless SSH management.
  • K3s server on deus, legion joined as agent; two nodes Ready.
  • First labels applied; test nginx workload served over NodePort.
  • Node names and IP scheme fixed: deus/.250, legion/.249, nebula/.248.

  • Monitoring stack (kube-prometheus-stack), MetalLB.
