docs.title: Week 3: Consolidating the Foundation, NAS Hardware, Monitoring, and Automation
docs.text:
Covers roughly 14 May – 7 June 2026. Phase 1 is done; this is everything between a working two-node cluster and the ZFS/Seafile build that opens June.

This was a longer, more diffuse stretch: the "make the foundation solid and observable" phase. I brought the desktop/NAS node (nebula) online through some hardware pain, stood up real node-health monitoring in Grafana, wrote the cluster power automation, and settled how I'd document the whole thing. By 7 June I had a genuinely instrumented, manageable cluster ready for the ZFS layer.

docs.title: 1. Phase 1 → Phase 2 handoff
docs.text:
Once the two-node cluster was serving workloads, I explicitly shifted mode: I told myself to stop asking for step-by-step hand-holding and start exploring independently, wanting high-level orientation rather than prescriptive instructions now that the system worked. Two concrete near-term milestones set here: buy a domain by end of week, stand up the NAS node by end of month.

The Phase 2 landscape (for orientation, not execution yet): external access via Cloudflare Tunnel + Traefik ingress (with the TLS-termination modes: flexible / full / full-strict, and proxy-vs-DNS-only tradeoffs to learn); storage, splitting into TrueNAS/NFS for bulk media vs Longhorn for distributed block storage behind stateful workloads; and Jellyfin as the first real portfolio workload. Natural sequence: Cloudflare + domain → a test service to validate the ingress chain → NAS → Jellyfin, with Longhorn and VLANs as independent side-explorations.

docs.title: 2. nebula: acquiring and reviving the desktop/NAS node
docs.text: The third node, nebula, is a second-hand desktop: i7-6700K, GTX 1080, 24GB RAM, Asus Z170 Pro. It doubles as the ZFS NAS and the Docker Compose host. Getting it running was the most hands-on hardware episode of the whole build.

docs.title: The boot-failure saga
docs.text:
After disassembling it for cleaning, it wouldn't boot: Windows showed nothing in the boot manager, and an Ubuntu Server installer crashed mid-install. I'd already replaced the CMOS battery. This turned out to be a reassembly problem, worked through in priority order:

  • RAM seating: top suspect, given the unusual 24GB config.
  • GPU seating + power connector.
  • SSD cable connections.
  • CPU cooler contact.

I fixed it by pulling and reseating the GPU and RAM. Exact root cause stayed unconfirmed, but the lesson stuck: after any disassembly, reseat everything before assuming a component died. Non-obvious boot failures are usually mechanical, not fatal.

docs.title: BIOS tuning for a 24/7 NAS
docs.text:
Since nebula runs always-on, I tuned the Z170 for efficiency: enable Intel SpeedStep/EIST and C-States (incl. C6/C7) and ErP Ready; optionally cap power by disabling Turbo Boost or lowering PL1/PL2; minor wins from disabling unused controllers and onboard LEDs. powertop in the OS to verify real draw. The board's "power efficient" preset covers most of this but can be beaten manually.

One hardware note: nebula's PSU is a CoolerMaster V750 Gold (750W): oversized for the load, so it runs at the inefficient low end of its curve (~5–8W extra loss at idle, minor in real cost). Flagged a right-sized 300–450W Gold unit as a someday-if-cheap swap, low priority.

docs.title: The GPU correction worth recording
docs.text: A recurring confusion I had to correct myself on: the discrete GPU (GTX 1080) is in nebula, but nebula is a Docker Compose host, not a K3s node. The only GPU on a K3s node is legion's GTX 1060. This matters enormously for Jellyfin placement: nebula has the better GPU and the integrated Intel HD 530 (good for QSV transcoding), but a K3s-scheduled Jellyfin pod can't reach either, because nebula isn't in the cluster. That tension (good GPU on the non-cluster node) is the Jellyfin question that stays open for months.

docs.title: 3. Node-health monitoring in Grafana
docs.text: With kube-prometheus-stack installed, I built a real node-health dashboard, the first serious observability work. This session also taught me a pile of cluster-access mechanics that became permanent knowledge.

docs.title: Access mechanics learned the hard way
docs.text:
• localhost vs LAN IP over SSH. Port-forwarding a ClusterIP service and trying to reach it was confusing until I understood: kubectl port-forward --address 0.0.0.0 … binds to all interfaces so I can hit it from Windows at the node's LAN IP (e.g. http://192.168.1.250:9090 for Prometheus). ClusterIP services aren't reachable externally without this. (This is the same SSH-localhost trap that recurs throughout the project.)
  • The kubeconfig permission fix. /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml is root-only by default. Fix: chmod 644 and add --write-kubeconfig-mode=644 to the K3s systemd service so it survives restarts. This is what later lets me scp the kubeconfig to my laptop without sudo.
  • Grafana confirmed on svc/kube-prom-grafana (ClusterIP :80), reached via port-forward 8080:80.

docs.title: Sensor discovery: what the hardware actually exposes
docs.text:
Rather than guess PromQL, I queried Prometheus to see which sensors returned data:

  • CPU temp works via node_hwmon_temp_celsius with the coretemp chip.
  • CPU voltage does not exist: node_hwmon_in_volts returned nothing; these boards don't expose voltage rails. Dropped from scope entirely.
  • RAPL power (node_rapl_package_joules_total) returned nothing from the container despite working at the host (sudo cat /sys/class/powercap/intel-rapl:0/energy_uj gave a real value). The fix: node-exporter needs runAsNonRoot: false / runAsUser: 0 in its securityContext to read RAPL. (This node-exporter-as-root theme comes back much later during the SSA/CRD work.)
  • A real thermal finding: deus's (M910q) NVMe temp2 sensor read ~89.85°C at idle, a genuine concern flagged for airflow attention. This is the earliest signal of the "deus runs hot" theme that later drives keeping Longhorn replicas off it.

Delivered: working PromQL for CPU usage/temp, RAM, network (with virtual-interface filtering), disk read/write, NVMe temp, plus a PrometheusRule with alerts (CPU critical >90°C for 2m, NVMe warning >80°C for 5m), wired to both Alertmanager and Grafana alerting. GPU panels deferred (legion's dGPU was disabled via envycontrol).

docs.title: 4. Cluster power automation
docs.text:
Because legion was still a come-and-go node, I wrote a pair of scripts to bring the cluster up and down cleanly: cluster-shutdown.sh and cluster-powerup.sh. These went through several meaningful refinements:

  • Shutdown (runs on deus): SSH into legion, poweroff, then shut down deus itself, but abort rather than proceed if the worker can't be confirmed offline, so deus never shuts down while a worker is stranded. A nuance: sudo systemctl poweroff over SSH usually drops the connection before returning a clean exit code, so a ping-based verification loop is the authoritative check, not the SSH exit status.
  • Powerup: send a Wake-on-LAN magic packet to legion, then poll the K3s API (kubectl get node) until legion reports Ready, a real readiness check, not just a ping.
  • Least-privilege security model: rather than blanket passwordless sudo, scoped /etc/sudoers.d/cluster-poweroff entries granting NOPASSWD only for systemctl poweroff on both machines, plus a dedicated SSH key (~/.ssh/cluster_shutdown) with BatchMode=yes so it fails cleanly instead of hanging on a prompt.

This is also where the identifiers leifsen (my username) and legion (the node) got locked in.

(Worth noting the arc: these WoL/shutdown scripts exist precisely because legion was transient. When I later pulled its battery and made it always-on, the scripts' importance faded, but the least-privilege sudoers/SSH pattern in them is still good practice I carried forward.)

docs.title: 5. Documentation strategy
docs.text:
I also settled how I'd record all this, which is why these very logs exist. Two categories:

  • Decision logs: short markdown entries written at decision time, capturing the reasoning behind architectural tradeoffs. These live in a /docs folder.
  • Polished technical write-ups: the "how" and lessons learned, meant as portfolio pieces.

GitHub is the non-negotiable source of truth for all of it. Self-hosting the docs on the cluster is a Phase 2–3 milestone, not the primary home, because cluster downtime during learning makes self-hosting unreliable as the sole destination. Plan: GitHub as canonical, GitHub Pages as fallback, and eventually a Hugo/Astro static site containerized and deployed through the CI/CD pipeline, so the deployment pipeline itself becomes a portfolio artifact.

docs.title: State at the end of this stretch (7 June)
docs.text:
• Three nodes online: deus (control plane, .250), legion (worker, .249), nebula (NAS/Compose host, .248, revived and BIOS-tuned).
  • Real node-health monitoring in Grafana with temperature alerting; sensor capabilities mapped; deus's hot NVMe already flagged.
  • Cluster power automation with a proper least-privilege model.
  • Documentation approach decided; GitHub as source of truth.
  • Key permanent lessons banked: kubeconfig write-kubeconfig-mode=644, the SSH-localhost trap, node-exporter-as-root for RAPL, "reseat before you panic," and the nebula-has-the-GPU-but-isn't-in-K3s tension.

docs.title: Open / next (this is where the June-8 logs pick up)
docs.text:
• ZFS pool on nebula, then Seafile via Docker Compose (the June 8 session).
  • CI/CD pipeline (the next major push).
  • Everything the "NAS owns data, K3s owns services" principle implies, including the still-unresolved Jellyfin GPU-placement question.

docs.title: Week 4: Planning Baseline and the First Real Questions
docs.text:
Covers roughly the week of 8 June 2026.

This is where I'm starting the written record. By this point the cluster wasn't a blank sheet. I'd already planned it out, bought the hardware, and had ZFS and Seafile running on nebula. So this first week is less "day one" and more "the point where I started asking the questions that actually shaped the build."

docs.title: Where things stood when I started writing this down
docs.text:
Three nodes, all on Ubuntu Server, all meant to be always-on:

  • deus: Lenovo M910q at 192.168.1.250. This is the control plane. It's the small always-on box, so anything that has to never go down lives here.
  • nebula: the i7-6700K desktop at 192.168.1.248. It has 24GB RAM, a GTX 1080, and it's my NAS. ZFS pool tank lives here, and Seafile runs on it via Docker Compose.
  • legion: a laptop at 192.168.1.249 with a GTX 1060. Early on I was still thinking of it as a "transient" node that might not always be up. That assumption changed later (I pulled the battery and it's now always-on), but at this point I was still treating it as flaky.

The guiding principle I'd already settled on: NAS owns data, K3s owns services. Seafile is the deliberate exception. It sits on Compose on nebula because it's a data-safety thing and I didn't want it depending on the cluster being healthy.

docs.title: The Jellyfin / GPU question
docs.text:
The first real architecture tension I hit. I want Jellyfin to be a K3s workload: it's a good portfolio artifact, it's the kind of thing that shows I can run a real service on the cluster. But GPU transcoding wants a GPU, and the GTX 1080 is in nebula, which is a Compose host, not a K3s node.

So there's a pull: the convenient place to run Jellyfin (where the good GPU is) is exactly the place that breaks my "K3s owns services" thesis, the same way Seafile already does.

What I learned digging into this:

  • GPU transcoding matters because it offloads the decode/encode work onto fixed-function NVENC/NVDEC silicon instead of hammering the CPU. That's what lets you run several simultaneous streams without the CPU falling over, and it's far more power-efficient.
  • Consumer GeForce cards have a driver-enforced 3-session NVENC cap. The 1080 included. There's a community patch that lifts it, which is worth remembering if I ever push past three concurrent transcodes.

I didn't resolve the placement question this week, neither was this service actually crucial for the cluster. The honest answer was: defer it until I'm actually deploying Jellyfin, because CI/CD was the more urgent next step. It's still an open question, legion has a GTX 1060 and is a K3s node, so GPU scheduling on legion (via the NVIDIA device plugin) is the alternative to caving and putting Jellyfin on nebula/Compose.

docs.title: The ArgoCD SSH port-forward gap
docs.text:
Right as I was about to start the CI/CD work, I caught a gap in my own setup guide. The guide said "run kubectl port-forward and open localhost:8080 in a browser." That instruction quietly assumes kubectl is running on my laptop. But I was doing everything over SSH into deus, so localhost there is deus's loopback, not my laptop's. The browser on my laptop can't reach a port that's only bound on deus's loopback.

This is the SSH-localhost trap and it bit me before I'd even really started. Three ways out:

  1. SSH tunnel: ssh -L 8080:localhost:8080 leifsen@192.168.1.250 chains my laptop's localhost through to the port-forward running on deus. Fastest for a one-off check.
  2. Bind to all interfaces: kubectl port-forward --address 0.0.0.0 ... then hit deus's LAN IP directly.
  3. Run kubectl locally: copy deus's kubeconfig (/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml) to the laptop and change the server: field from 127.0.0.1 to 192.168.1.250. This is the clean long-term fix and it means I stop SSHing in for routine kubectl work entirely.

I flagged option 3 as the real answer, and it's exactly what I set up properly a couple of weeks later.

docs.title: What I decided this week
docs.text:
• Jellyfin placement: deferred, revisit at deploy time. Don't cave to nebula reflexively; legion + NVIDIA device plugin is the K3s-honest path.
  • Next focus: CI/CD. Everything else waits behind getting a real git push → deploy loop working.
  • Cluster access: move to a local kubeconfig so I'm not trapped in SSH.

docs.title: Still open going into next week
docs.text:
• Full GitOps CI/CD pipeline (the immediate next thing).
  • Jellyfin GPU placement.
  • legion's real status (still "transient" in my head at this point).

docs.title: Week 5: CI/CD Goes Live, Networking Gets Real, Dev Containers Appear
docs.text:
Covers roughly 10–15 June 2026. This was the heaviest week by far.

Four big things landed this week: the full GitOps pipeline, the decision to add WireGuard/Tailscale alongside Cloudflare, the first dev container (with a nasty security surprise), plus some hardware and cost sanity-checking. I'll take them in order.

docs.title: 1. The full CI/CD pipeline: the centerpiece
docs.text:
This is the thing I'd been building toward. The goal was a working loop:

git push → GitHub Actions builds image → ghcr.io → ArgoCD syncs → pod rolls over

I built it from ArgoCD upward rather than trying to wire the whole thing at once. (Claude and I initially got tangled trying to do it top-down; I flagged the confusion and we restarted from "get ArgoCD reconciling something first," which was the right call.)

docs.title: The order it actually went
docs.text:
1. Expose ArgoCD via a Traefik IngressRoute and a Cloudflare tunnel. deus runs its own cloudflared systemd daemon, separate from the one on nebula that serves Seafile. The tunnel points at localhost:80 (Traefik), hostname argocd.packetcraft.dev.
  2. Beat the .dev HSTS problem. .dev is HSTS-preloaded, so browsers refuse self-signed certs outright. The fix is to route through the Cloudflare tunnel, which terminates TLS at Cloudflare's edge with a real cert. This is why the tunnel isn't optional for .dev domains; it's not just convenience.
  3. Validate the reconciliation loop with a throwaway guestbook Application before trusting it with anything real.
  4. Wire the two-repo pipeline properly.

docs.title: The two-repo pattern (and why it has to be two)
docs.text:
• BarneyLaw/nginx-app: source + the CI workflow.
  • BarneyLaw/homelab-cicd-config: the Kustomize manifests ArgoCD watches.

The reason it's two repos and not one: CI writes back to the config repo. If the app repo and the config repo were the same repo, that write-back commit would re-trigger CI, which would write back again, an infinite build loop. Splitting them breaks the loop. CI writes to config; ArgoCD reads from config; the app repo is never touched by automation.

The seam between them is the Kustomize images: block. CI runs kustomize edit set image ...=<image>:<sha> which surgically rewrites the tag. ArgoCD sees the commit and applies it. I never hand-edit the image line.

docs.title: Bugs I hit and fixed (all real, all annoying)
docs.text:
• Config repo name mismatch: the workflow referenced homelab-config but the repo is homelab-cicd-config. Checkout failed until I fixed the name.
  • Uppercase owner in the ghcr image: BarneyLaw vs required barneylaw. ghcr.io rejects uppercase repo names, and worse, kustomize edit set image does a case-sensitive string match, so a case mismatch silently matches nothing and the tag never updates. Fixed by forcing lowercase with tr in the workflow.
  • Swapped file contents between kustomization.yaml and service.yaml. Kustomize specifically reads the file named kustomization.yaml, so swapping contents breaks it silently.

docs.title: Credentials: the part that's easy to get wrong
docs.text:
Three boundaries, each needs a credential only when it crosses into private:

  • CI → ghcr.io (push): built-in GITHUB_TOKEN + declaring packages: write. No manual setup.
  • CI → config repo (write tag): CONFIG_REPO_TOKEN, a fine-grained PAT scoped to only homelab-cicd-config, Contents read/write, nothing else. This is the one I have to make by hand. One PAT works for every app repo since they all write to the same config repo; I just add it as a secret in each.
  • Cluster → ghcr.io (pull): only needed if the package is private. Start by making it public to validate the loop, switch to an image pull secret later.

By the end of the session I had a green end-to-end sync visible in the ArgoCD UI, and I turned the whole thing into a generalized setup guide (cicd-pipeline-setup-guide.md) so standing up any new service is a checklist, not a re-derivation.

docs.title: CI at scale (a follow-up question)
docs.text:
I asked whether ten different code-server toolchain variants (React, Flutter, Java, etc.) would need ten repos. Answer: no, one app repo with a build matrix. The two-repo split is source-vs-config, not one-repo-per-image. To keep build times sane at that scale:

  • Path-based filtering (paths: triggers + dorny/paths-filter) so only changed variants rebuild.
  • Shared base image: one base/Dockerfile with code-server + common tools, per-toolchain Dockerfiles do FROM base.
  • GHA layer caching with scoped cache-from/cache-to (type=gha).
  • Matrix jobs run parallel (up to 20 on free tier), so a full rebuild's wall-clock is roughly one build. The catch is free-tier minutes get eaten when the base changes; Flutter's SDK is the specific slow layer to order carefully.

docs.title: 2. Networking: Cloudflare Tunnel isn't enough on its own
docs.text:
I'd noticed the Cloudflare Tunnel is slow for bulk transfers. That's not a misconfiguration; it's structural. Traffic hairpins out to a Cloudflare edge PoP and back, so file transfers (Seafile, eventually Jellyfin, obsync) pay a detour.

The original reason I was on Cloudflare Tunnel at all: Singtel gives me a locked router with no port-forwarding or DHCP control, so inbound ports weren't an option. The tunnel dials outbound, which sidesteps that.

The plan that came out of this was a hybrid split:

  • Cloudflare Tunnel stays for low-bandwidth public services: the planned Hugo/Astro docs site, the ArgoCD UI. It's a dumb pipe and that's fine for those.
  • WireGuard / Tailscale for high-throughput stuff: Seafile, Jellyfin, obsync, bulk transfers.

Options weighed:

  1. WireGuard mesh via a cheap VPS relay (home dials out, no inbound ports needed).
  2. Tailscale / Headscale: WireGuard under the hood, but with built-in NAT traversal and DERP relay fallback. Identified as the lowest-effort high-bandwidth option specifically because of the locked-router constraint.
  3. Cloudflare WARP-to-Tunnel private routing, noted as not solving the bandwidth problem (still hairpins).

The principle I locked in here: Cloudflare Tunnel = dumb pipe, Traefik = routing brain. Both Cloudflare and Tailscale are just ingress pipes feeding the same Traefik routing layer. This becomes a recurring rule.

docs.title: 3. The first dev container, and a security surprise
docs.text:
I built a dynamically-scheduled VS Code dev container (code-server) on the cluster through the GitOps pipeline. Two repos again: code-server-app (source + CI) and the shared config repo. The point was a reproducible dev environment and a sandbox for running an autonomous coding agent (OpenAI Codex).

This session was a gauntlet of small real failures, each with a lesson:

  1. CI didn't trigger: code-server-app was initialized locally with a master default branch, but the workflow watched main. Each repo tracks its branch independently; my config repo uses main, this one came up master.
  2. VS Code CLI Dockerfile layer 404'd: the code.visualstudio.com/sha/... redirect endpoint is fragile. Fixed by switching to the stable update.code.visualstudio.com/latest/cli-linux-x64/stable URL.
  3. Crash loop: entrypoint.sh was committed from Windows without the executable bit. Fixed with --chmod=755 on the COPY.
  4. code tunnel rejected --random-name=false: it's a presence/absence boolean flag, not one that takes a value.
  5. Auth didn't survive pod restarts: the PVC was mounted at ~/.vscode-cli but the CLI actually writes to ~/.vscode/cli. Found by running find /home/dev/.vscode -maxdepth 3 instead of assuming the path.
  6. Tunnel re-registered as a new service every deploy: fixed by pinning the pod to nebula with nodeSelector and correcting the PVC mountPath.

Codex's ChatGPT login needs a browser callback a headless pod can't do, so I transplanted the credential file: scp to deus, then kubectl cp into the pod's persistent ~/.codex PVC.

docs.title: The ambient authority leak
docs.text:
The scary one. The container could git push to GitHub with no configured credentials, no stored token, a clean remote URL. That shouldn't be possible.

Cause: GIT_ASKPASS and related VSCODE_GIT_* env vars set by the VS Code server. They broker git credential requests through my signed-in editor session, giving the agent implicit, account-wide GitHub write access instead of repo-scoped access. All my careful network and filesystem scoping didn't matter, because the credential came in through a side channel inherited from the editor.

The fix (fine-grained single-repo PAT via a Kubernetes Secret + unsetting the VS Code git env vars) I deliberately deferred: current state is fine for supervised runs only. I wrote up twelve numbered lessons and an open-items checklist. This leak comes back the following week.

docs.title: Storage decision baked in here
docs.text: The pod is pinned to nebula, not dynamically placed, because local-path PVs are node-bound and a stateful interactive workload needs either node-independent storage or a pin. Dynamic placement is for stateless services. Longhorn is the correct long-term fix to get free placement back with persistent storage, and it's now unblocked since the NAS drives are in with ZFS running. The workspace itself stays ephemeral (emptyDir, wiped on restart); only the auth dirs (~/.vscode/cli, ~/.codex) persist on small 64Mi PVCs.

docs.title: 4. Hardware and cost sanity checks
docs.text:
Two side conversations that informed direction:

Cheap interconnect / more nodes. The cluster had drifted from "many cheap nodes" toward "fewer, more powerful nodes." To reintroduce breadth without breaking my single-arch (linux/amd64) images, the zero-friction path is Intel N100/N150 mini-PCs (Beelink S12 Pro, GMKtec G3, Trigkey) or used USFF enterprise boxes (ThinkCentre M710q/M910q, HP EliteDesk 800 G3/G4). ARM SBCs like Raspberry Pis would force multi-arch builds via docker buildx, avoidable friction. (I also floated a separate 10-node Pi cluster for CS3210 parallel-computing coursework; for MPI-from-source the arch concern disappears, but old Pis with 100Mbit ethernet would bottleneck collective ops; Pi 3B+/4 with gigabit is the educational choice.)

AWS-equivalent cost. As a sanity check on whether owning hardware was worth it: the cluster (deus 4c/16GB, nebula 8c/24GB+1080, legion 6c/16GB+1060, ~1TB ZFS) maps to roughly $970/month / $11,600/year on-demand, ~$7,000/year on 1-year reserved. My entire hardware build cost less than one month of that bill. Electricity is ~S$15–35/month for the always-on nodes, which is fine. The broader lesson: cloud wins for spiky/unpredictable load, owned hardware wins for steady high-utilization baselines, which is exactly the deus-always-on / burst-elsewhere shape I already have.

docs.title: What I locked in this week
docs.text:
• CI/CD pipeline is live and documented. Two-repo pattern, SHA-tagged images, ArgoCD self-heal/prune.
  • Hybrid networking direction: Cloudflare for public/low-bandwidth, WireGuard/Tailscale for bulk. Tailscale is the front-runner given the locked router.
  • Dev container running but with a known, deferred credential leak. Supervised use only until fixed.
  • Longhorn is the next storage unlock now that NAS drives are in.

docs.title: Still open
docs.text:
• The GIT_ASKPASS credential leak (deferred, comes back next week).
  • Actually deploying WireGuard/Tailscale (planned, not done).
  • Longhorn install.
  • Jellyfin placement (still open from Week 1).

docs.title: Week 6: Clean Cluster Access, Documentation, Closing the Security Hole, WireGuard
docs.text:
Covers roughly 15–21 June 2026.

This week was about consolidating. The pipeline worked, so now I made the cluster pleasant to operate (proper kubectl access), wrote down what I'd learned (a run of reference guides), finally closed the credential leak from last week, and got WireGuard actually deployed.

docs.title: 1. Proper cluster access from my real machine
docs.text:
I was tired of SSHing into nodes for everything. The conceptual split I settled on and want to keep straight:

  • Node-level work → SSH. Anything below K3s: the OS, systemd, ZFS, installing the k3s binary itself.
  • Cluster-level work → kubectl against the API server. Deploying, debugging, inspecting workloads.

These are different layers and I shouldn't be reaching for SSH to do cluster-level things.

docs.title: The Windows/WSL setup
docs.text:
I work from a Windows PC, doing terminal and kubectl work in WSL. Setup:

  • Install just kubectl on the client (not the whole k3s binary): winget install -e --id Kubernetes.kubectl.
  • Bootstrap the kubeconfig in one shot: ssh leifsen@192.168.1.250 "sudo cat /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml" > ~/.kube/config
  • Edit the server: field from https://127.0.0.1:6443 to https://192.168.1.250:6443.
  • Added k9s (winget install Derailed.k9s) for a terminal UI over the cluster.

Two gotchas that will silently break this:

  1. TLS SAN: the API server's cert has to include 192.168.1.250 in its SANs, or kubectl refuses the connection. Fixed on deus via --tls-san in the k3s server config; this is a server-side fix, not something I can patch on the client.
  2. WARP split-tunnel: for remote (off-LAN) access, WARP must not exclude RFC1918 ranges, or the private route to 192.168.1.0/24 gets dropped. The neat payoff: with the tunnel advertising the private route, the same kubeconfig works both on-LAN and remotely with no reconfiguration.

docs.title: The workflow rule this reinforces
docs.text:
Because ArgoCD runs with selfHeal: true, any manual kubectl edit on a managed workload gets reverted. So:

  • Managed app changes → git push to the config repo. That's the source of truth.
  • kubectl / k9s → live debugging and cluster ops only.

Don't fight self-heal. If I want a change to stick, it goes in git.

docs.title: 2. A run of reference documentation
docs.text:
I wrote several guides this week, in the same house style as the CI/CD guide (ASCII diagrams, comparison tables, blockquote warnings, dependency-ordered checklists, a command reference at the end). These are for future-me.

  • Dockerfile guide: every major instruction, the layer-caching mental model, the cleanup-in-the-same-RUN rule, dependency-before-source ordering, base image trade-offs (scratch / distroless / alpine / -slim), multi-stage patterns. Tailored to my actual projects: the obsync-server binary with its serve | migrate | health subcommands (hence the ENTRYPOINT ["/server"] + CMD ["serve"] pattern and the CGO_ENABLED=0 requirement for a scratch final stage), plus the custom L4/L7 proxy and scheduler. Noted the Node→nginx multi-stage pattern for the upcoming static docs site, and that off-the-shelf images (Jellyfin, Grafana) skip CI entirely.

  • K3s / Kubernetes guide: fourteen sections answering "are K3s and Kubernetes the same thing" and everything downstream: the reconciliation mental model, the object hierarchy, kubectl, manifest anatomy, scheduling (nodeSelector, affinity, taints/tolerations, resource requests), networking (Service types, the Cloudflare Tunnel ingress path, CoreDNS, Flannel), storage (PVC/PV/SC, local-path vs planned Longhorn), ConfigMaps/Secrets, probes, Helm vs Kustomize, K3s-specific ops. Every concept tied back to my actual architecture. Flagged the NVIDIA device plugin as the missing link for GPU scheduling on legion, which is the key that would let Jellyfin run on legion in-cluster instead of caving to nebula/Compose.

  • Observability setup guide (this leans into next week's monitoring work, but the writing happened here). Covered the Prometheus Operator's ServiceMonitor CRD model and the serviceMonitorSelector label-matching gotcha: if the selector doesn't match your ServiceMonitor's labels, scrapes silently fail. The RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) as the per-service dashboard framework. Traefik metrics via K3s HelmChartConfig (with addRoutersLabels / addServicesLabels for per-hostname breakdown). Two open decisions written down explicitly: the permissive serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false toggle vs labelling every ServiceMonitor, and PVC vs GitOps-managed ConfigMaps for Grafana dashboards (I lean ConfigMaps, consistent with "GitHub as source of truth"). Decided to start by instrumenting existing services (Traefik, ArgoCD, Seafile) rather than new ones. KEDA autoscaling and the Seafile cross-boundary scrape are deferred as their own projects.

docs.title: 3. Closing the dev container security hole
docs.text:
Back to the GIT_ASKPASS leak from last week. This session I did the full upgrade pass on the dev container and actually closed it.

First, some housekeeping bugs found live:

  • A missing YAML --- separator meant the Codex auth PVC (code-server-codex-auth) was never created; only one PVC existed instead of two. So Codex credentials were living on ephemeral storage, one pod restart from being lost. Fixed the separator, backed up auth.json, committed the PVC fix.
  • Confirmed the tunnel auth was correctly persisted at ~/.vscode/cli.

docs.title: The architectural decision: one container = one project
docs.text: Each dev environment gets its own repo and its own scoped GitHub PAT. I built a generator (new-project-env.sh + four YAML templates in code-server-app/templates/), derived faithfully from the live deployment rather than a speculative redesign. It takes <PROJECT>, <REPO_URL>, branch, tunnel name, image name; substitutes placeholders; and prints the exact out-of-band steps (PAT creation, scope verification). First instantiation: budget-app-dev.

docs.title: Two distinct security holes, confirmed by testing
docs.text:
1. The env-var leak is structural. GIT_ASKPASS / VSCODE_GIT_* are injected by the VS Code tunnel server into child shells after the entrypoint runs, so unsetting them in the entrypoint can't reach the agent's shells. I confirmed the account-wide access with an isolation test: GIT_ASKPASS= git -c core.askPass= ls-remote still returned refs.
  2. The PAT was scoped too broadly ("all repositories"), so even without the env leak the token itself was over-privileged.

The fixes are independent:

  • Re-mint the PAT scoped to a single repo (GitHub-side, no rebuild needed). This is the load-bearing security fix.
  • Dockerfile changes to close the env leak everywhere shells can start:
  • /etc/profile.d/devbox-path.sh for interactive login shells.
  • /etc/devbox-bashenv.sh referenced via ENV BASH_ENV= for non-interactive bash -c shells; this is the path Codex actually uses, which is why entrypoint-only unsets missed it.
  • git config --system core.askPass "" at system level as environment-independent defense.

docs.title: Toolchain upgrades (same session)
docs.text: The code-server-app image grew a Flutter environment for a budget-app project: Flutter SDK 3.27.1 (added as the dev user, precache --universal), OpenJDK 17, Android cmdline-tools with the critical cmdline-tools/latest/ layout fix that sdkmanager requires, and platform-tools (adb) pulled non-fatally at build. Heavy Android bits (platforms;android-34, build-tools) deliberately deferred to runtime via sdkmanager; I chose "Java + cmdline-tools only" explicitly. System Gradle omitted on purpose since Flutter projects vendor their own gradlew. The image stays a monolith for now rather than splitting into per-toolchain variants, a deliberate "get it running" choice.

docs.title: 4. WireGuard actually gets deployed
docs.text:
Following the hybrid-networking plan from last week, I moved on WireGuard for the bulk-transfer path. The question that gates everything: is my Singtel line behind CGNAT, or do I have a real public IP? A fully home-owned WireGuard setup (no VPS) only works with a real routable IP.

I shared my WAN IP and it checked out; it belongs to the SINGTEL-FIBRE 42.60.0.0–42.61.255.255 allocation (SingNET Broadband), a genuine public IP, not in the 100.64.x.x CGNAT range. So a no-VPS setup is possible in principle.

The remaining unknown: will the locked Singtel ONR forward inbound UDP 51820 to deus? I tried testing with nc -u from my phone on mobile data and got nothing, but that result is inconclusive, not a failure. The most likely reason for silence was that I hadn't actually added a port-forward rule to the ONR yet, not that the ONR can't forward.

The better approach, which I took: stop messing with nc and just deploy the real WireGuard config on deus and the phone, then use a successful handshake (sudo wg show) as the definitive port-reachability test. That collapses the diagnostic and the deployment into one step. Also flagged: if the IP turns out dynamic, a Cloudflare DNS record (vpn.packetcraft.dev) updated via the Cloudflare API is the DDNS workaround.

(End state on the network stack, consolidated later: Tailscale subnet router on deus advertising 192.168.1.0/24, plus WireGuard on UDP 51820 port-forwarded through the ONR as the high-throughput admin path. WireGuard on UDP 51820 is confirmed working through the ONR; the real IP made it possible.)

docs.title: 5. Terraform vs Ansible: deciding the IaC layer
docs.text:
I asked whether to adopt Terraform or Ansible, and when. The distinction: Terraform provisions infrastructure via APIs; Ansible configures machines that already exist.

Decision: Ansible is the higher-value tool for me, because my manual-over-SSH work is exactly node/OS-layer config: k3s install with --tls-san, systemd units, ZFS setup, sudoers, WoL, kubeconfig distribution. The k3s-ansible role is a maintained starting point. Terraform is only narrowly useful here, for Cloudflare resources (tunnels, DNS, Zero Trust) and maybe GitHub config, but not for compute, since I have no API-driven provisioning.

The layering boundary I locked in: Ansible handles below-K3s node state, ArgoCD owns in-cluster workloads, and the two must not overlap.

On timing: don't adopt either mid-build. Write playbooks retroactively the next time I rebuild or add a node: capture the state when I'm already touching it, rather than stopping everything to Ansible-ify a working cluster. (Importing existing Cloudflare config into Terraform state is fiddly and better done incrementally anyway.)

docs.title: What I locked in this week
docs.text:
• Clean kubectl/k9s access from WSL, same config on-LAN and remote. TLS SAN and WARP split-tunnel are the two things that break it.
  • A shelf of reference guides (Docker, K3s, observability) in a consistent style.
  • Dev container security actually fixed: single-repo PAT (load-bearing) plus Dockerfile-level env-var closure at all shell entry points.
  • WireGuard deployed, using the handshake itself as the port test. Real public IP confirmed.
  • Ansible chosen as the IaC layer, to be written retroactively; ArgoCD/Ansible boundary drawn.

docs.title: Still open
docs.text:
• Longhorn (still not installed, comes next week).
  • Grafana/Prometheus expansion beyond the guide (monitoring buildout).
  • Jellyfin placement (still open).
  • The reverse-proxy question that Tailscale raises (does adding it mean a second proxy? Resolved next week).

docs.title: Week 7: Ingress Architecture, Patch Management, and Longhorn
docs.text:
Covers roughly 25–26 June 2026.

Shorter week in terms of number of sessions, but it settled two architectural rules I'd been circling (ingress and patching) and finally kicked off Longhorn, which had been "next" for a while.

docs.title: 1. Should I run two reverse proxies?
docs.text:
The Tailscale work raised a real question: I've got Traefik handling traffic from the Cloudflare tunnels. Should I stand up a separate nginx to handle traffic coming in over Tailscale?

The answer I landed on: the two-pipe, one-brain model. Two ingress paths (Cloudflare and Tailscale) is fine, but they should both feed the same Traefik routing layer. Cloudflare and Tailscale are dumb pipes; Traefik is the single routing brain. This is the same principle from the networking week, now stated as a hard rule.

The important distinction, when is a second proxy acceptable:

  • Not acceptable: a second general-purpose in-cluster ingress controller running in parallel with Traefik. That's two brains, and routing logic fragments across both. Avoid.
  • Acceptable: nginx as an app-local front door for a self-contained stack that runs outside K3s. The obsync v2 design is exactly this: nginx scoped to the WireGuard interface, fronting the specific obsync-server/Postgres stack. That's analogous to how Seafile runs on Compose outside the cluster. The nginx there isn't a general ingress; it's part of one stack and never allowed to become a second general-purpose front door.

So the rule: per-app proxies must be scoped to their stack only. One general-purpose routing brain (Traefik), full stop.

docs.title: 2. Patch management without blind cron jobs
docs.text: I asked how to handle the endless stream of OS updates without running risky "blind upgrade" cron jobs. The framing that made it click: updates fall into three layers, each with its own strategy.

docs.title: Host OS packages
docs.text:
• unattended-upgrades scoped to security updates only, with auto-reboot disabled. I don't want a node silently rebooting itself mid-workload.
  • needrestart to identify which patches actually need a reboot, so reboots are a deliberate decision.
  • kured (Kubernetes Reboot Daemon) to automate the cordon → drain → reboot → uncordon cycle safely across the cluster when a reboot is needed. It coordinates so nodes don't all go down at once.

docs.title: K3s itself
docs.text: Version-pin and upgrade manually and deliberately. No automation here; a k3s version bump is not something I want happening unattended.

docs.title: In-cluster workloads
docs.text: My GitOps loop already handles this cleanly. The addition: Renovate to surface new image tags and Helm chart versions as pull requests against homelab-cicd-config, which then feed the normal ArgoCD reconciliation. So updates become reviewable PRs, not surprises.

docs.title: The nebula nuance
docs.text:
nebula is the awkward node: it runs Seafile, ZFS, and Compose workloads outside K3s. That means:

  • kured can't cordon/drain it the way it handles the K3s nodes, so suppressing auto-reboot matters most here.
  • Compose services on nebula should use restart: unless-stopped for resilience across any reboot that does happen.

(Renovate is noted as planned, not yet set up.)

docs.title: 3. sudoedit: a small quality-of-life recovery
docs.text: I remembered installing something in a past session that let me edit privileged files with a normal editor instead of sudo nvim, and wanted to find it. Turns out it wasn't a thing I installed; it's sudoedit, a built-in. It copies the privileged file to a temp location, lets me edit it as a normal user (with my own Neovim/LazyVim config, EDITOR=nvim), then writes it back with elevated privileges. Nothing to install; just use sudoedit /path/to/file. Worth writing down so I don't hunt for it again.

docs.title: 4. Longhorn: distributed storage, finally started
docs.text: The motivation has been consistent since the dev-container week: K3s's default local-path StorageClass pins stateful pods to a node via nodeSelector (the code-server pin to nebula is the live example). Longhorn gives replicated, distributed block storage with a proper CSI driver, which lets pods schedule node-independently while keeping persistent state.

docs.title: Prerequisites and the multipathd snag
docs.text:
Ran the official environment check:

curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/longhorn/longhorn/v1.8.1/scripts/environment_check.sh | bash

It flagged multipathd running on all three nodes, a known Longhorn breakage. multipath is an enterprise SAN feature with zero applicability to my directly-attached storage. Fix is either blacklisting sd* devices in /etc/multipath.conf or disabling the daemon outright (systemctl disable --now multipathd).

A subtlety that tripped me: deus already had the correct blacklist stanza in /etc/multipath.conf, but the warning persisted. That's because the environment check warns on the daemon being present at all, regardless of config, so I needed a reload/restart or a full disable to clear it, not just the right config file.

Longhorn installed after that and the web UI came up.

docs.title: The critical prerequisite gap: Longhorn cannot use ZFS
docs.text:
The big correctness point. Longhorn can't use a ZFS dataset as its data path. It needs a dedicated disk formatted ext4 or XFS, mounted at a stable path (e.g. /var/lib/longhorn-disk). So the ZFS tank mirror on nebula is not usable for Longhorn; I need separate disks.

This is why the plan settled the way it did:

  • nebula: dedicated Longhorn NVMe disk (separate from the ZFS pool), replica target.
  • legion: its 500GB WD Red SA500 SATA SSD partitioned, ~400GB for Longhorn at /var/lib/longhorn-disk-sda, replica target.
  • deus: no Longhorn replicas. deus overheats, and I don't want to add storage-replication load to it. Thermal management drives workload placement here.
  • 2 replicas (nebula NVMe + legion SATA). Two is the meaningful-redundancy floor; below two, Longhorn gives no node-independent redundancy at all.

docs.title: Related things flagged
docs.text:
• Security: the Longhorn UI was exposed via a Cloudflare tunnel without auth. Securing it got deferred to the next day, but it's noted.
  • Backup target: should point at an NFS share on nebula's ZFS tank pool, and this should be configured before any database holds meaningful data.
  • Replica count honesty: set it based on how many nodes actually have dedicated Longhorn disks. A single-node setup forces replica count 1 or produces perpetually degraded volumes; don't pretend to redundancy I don't have.
  • The payoff: once validated with a throwaway PVC, I can finally drop the nodeSelector pin on code-server and let it schedule freely.

docs.title: A note on legion's status
docs.text: Somewhere around here legion stopped being "transient" in my head. I pulled its battery and it runs all the time now. That's what makes it a legitimate Longhorn replica target and an always-on worker; I should stop treating it as WoL/transient. (Related: MetalLB advertising the Traefik VIP on legion is acceptable precisely because legion is now always-on.)

docs.title: What I locked in this week
docs.text:
• Ingress rule: two pipes (Cloudflare + Tailscale), one brain (Traefik). App-local proxies only for out-of-cluster stacks, scoped to that stack.
  • Patch strategy: three layers: unattended-upgrades (security, no reboot) + kured for host; manual pinned upgrades for K3s; Renovate PRs for workloads. nebula is the special case.
  • sudoedit for privileged file editing. Built-in, no install.
  • Longhorn installed, 2-replica across nebula NVMe + legion SATA, none on deus (thermal). ZFS-can't-back-Longhorn is the load-bearing constraint.
  • legion promoted from transient to always-on worker.

docs.title: Still open (carried forward)
docs.text:
• Secure the Longhorn UI (deferred to "next day").
  • Configure the Longhorn backup target (NFS on tank) before real DB data lands.
  • Validate with a throwaway PVC, then drop the code-server nodeSelector pin.
  • Grafana admin password → SealedSecret migration; the hand-applied Grafana lab. IngressRoute drift; the ArgoCD CRD annotations: Too long fix (resource-level ServerSideApply); these surface as the monitoring stack matures.
  • GitHub webhook for push-triggered ArgoCD sync (still on poll interval).
  • Jellyfin placement (still, genuinely, open).
  • obsync build, deliberately deferred until after the portfolio site, to avoid layering Go + Postgres + a hand-written sync protocol all at once.

docs.title: Week 8: The Two-Plane Ingress, Wildcard TLS, and Adopting Everything into GitOps
docs.text:
Covers roughly 27 June – 1 July 2026.

This was the week the network architecture actually took its final shape. Up to now I had "Cloudflare for public, WireGuard/Tailscale for bulk" as a direction. This week I turned it into a concrete two-plane ingress split with real wildcard TLS, moved secrets into Git properly, and started dragging my hand-installed Helm releases under ArgoCD so nothing is untracked.

docs.title: 1. The VPS relay question, and why I probably don't need it
docs.text:
I started the week pricing a cheap VPS to run a WireGuard relay, in case the locked Singtel ONR wouldn't forward inbound ports. What I learned about picking one: for a WireGuard relay, CPU and RAM barely matter (it runs fine on 512MB); the only things that matter are a high/unmetered bandwidth allowance and a 1Gbps+ port. BuyVM's Slice 512 (~$2/month annual, genuinely unmetered on 1Gbps) was the pick, with the caveat that stock is often unavailable. Also: put the VPS in an Asian region, not the US, or I'm compounding trans-Pacific latency from Singapore.

But the real conclusion was: I probably don't need the VPS at all. My Singtel line has a real routable public IP (confirmed back in Week 3), so if the ONR forwards UDP 51820 to deus, a direct WireGuard config is strictly better and free. Try the direct path first; treat a wg show handshake as proof.

docs.title: 2. The two-plane ingress split (the big architectural decision)
docs.text:
This is the one that mattered. I set up Tailscale for private access and, in doing so, settled the clean split I'd been circling:

  • *.packetcraft.dev: public, via Cloudflare Tunnel (outbound-only, no inbound port).
  • *.lab.packetcraft.dev: tailnet-only. Grey-cloud (DNS-only) A records in Cloudflare pointing at the private/Tailscale IPs, plus a Tailscale split-DNS entry forwarding the zone to 1.1.1.1 so the OS resolver actually works.

The correction that shaped this: MagicDNS can't hold arbitrary custom records. I'd assumed I could just use Tailscale's own DNS for the lab. names, but it doesn't work that way, so Cloudflare public DNS serves as the record store even for the tailnet-only names. The records just resolve to private IPs that only mean anything if you're on the tailnet.

Two more decisions here:

  • Seafile stays on Cloudflare Tunnel, not Tailscale. It's a >6-user use case and that doesn't fit the tailnet model (I'd have to enroll every user's device). Public tunnel is the right call for it.
  • The lab. zone needs a real Let's Encrypt wildcard cert, not self-signed, because .dev is HSTS-preloaded; browsers hard-block plaintext HTTP with no click-through. Same HSTS lesson from the CI/CD week, now applying to the private plane too.

docs.title: 3. Wildcard TLS via cert-manager + Let's Encrypt DNS-01
docs.text:
To get that wildcard cert for *.lab.packetcraft.dev, I set up cert-manager with a DNS-01 challenge against Cloudflare. This is where I hit the most confusing debugging loop of the week, and the lesson is worth writing down carefully:

The Cloudflare API token SealedSecret has to live in the right namespace, and "the right namespace" is different for the issuer input vs the cert output.

  • The API token (the issuer's input) must be in the cert-manager namespace, because cert-manager runs with --cluster-resource-namespace=$(POD_NAMESPACE), so a ClusterIssuer looks for its credentials there.
  • The cert output (for the TLSStore) lives in kube-system.

I had the token sealed for the wrong namespace, so the DNS-01 challenge kept failing. Different rules for issuer-input vs cert-output is the thing to remember. (SealedSecrets are encrypted per namespace+name, so a namespace mismatch = decryption failure, full stop.)

Also, embarrassingly simple: at one point the SealedSecret file was generated but never kubectl apply'd. Generating the sealed file isn't the same as applying it. Easy to lose an hour to that.

docs.title: 4. Sealed Secrets: secrets in Git, done right
docs.text:
Tied to the TLS work, I leaned into Sealed Secrets as the way to keep credentials in Git safely. The controller encrypts SealedSecret objects that only the in-cluster controller can decrypt, so they're safe to commit. Three disciplines this demands:

  • Namespace scoping: encrypted per namespace+name; mismatches silently fail to decrypt (exactly what bit me with cert-manager).
  • existingSecret pattern: migrate service credentials to reference a secret instead of letting the Helm chart own them. Grafana's admin password is the poster child (more on that in Week 6/7).
  • Back up the controller's private key: outside the cluster and outside Git. If I lose it, every sealed secret is unrecoverable. The command: kubectl get secret -n kube-system -l sealedsecrets.bitnami.com/sealed-secrets-key -o yaml.

I confirmed I don't need a heavier secrets manager (Vault, External Secrets Operator) yet; those only earn their place if I need dynamic secrets, rotation, or audit logging. For obsync's Postgres creds and per-device tokens, Sealed Secrets is right.

docs.title: 5. Adopting hand-installed Helm releases into GitOps
docs.text:
I'd installed kube-prometheus-stack and ArgoCD itself by hand. This week I started adopting them into ArgoCD Applications so they're tracked, not drift.

A couple of concrete snags:

  • Release-name mismatch nearly created a duplicate. The live kube-prometheus-stack release is actually named kube-prom, not kube-prometheus-stack. Adopting under the wrong name would have stood up a second, conflicting release. Match the existing release name exactly.
  • The ArgoCD server.insecure flag goes under configs.params, not under server:. I had it in the wrong place. (It needs to run insecure/HTTP so Traefik + Cloudflare own TLS, otherwise redirect loop, same lesson as the CI/CD guide.)

docs.title: The GitOps pattern this clarified
docs.text:
This is where I nailed down the repo conventions:

  • Pattern B (upstream Helm charts): just an argocd/<svc>.yaml Application file. No apps/<svc>/ folder needed.
  • apps/<svc>/ only exists when I author manifests myself.
  • Multi-source when a chart needs my own values + optional custom manifests: chart repo + a $values ref from homelab-cicd-config + an optional custom manifests source.

docs.title: 6. Cleanup: orphaned nginx and guestbook
docs.text: Housekeeping. The old nginx and guestbook test workloads were still running even though I thought I'd removed them. The lesson: deleting an ArgoCD Application does not cascade-prune the live resources unless specific conditions are met, so they were orphaned plain Kubernetes objects with no controller recreating them (and none resurrecting them either, since the Applications were already gone). I confirmed only budget-app-dev and code-server remained as Applications, then cleaned up with kubectl delete ns nginx guestbook and checked the apps/nginx/ and apps/guestbook/ folders were gone from the config repo so nothing could accidentally resurrect them.

docs.title: What I locked in this week
docs.text:
• Two-plane ingress: *.packetcraft.dev public via Cloudflare, *.lab.packetcraft.dev tailnet-only via grey-cloud records + Tailscale split-DNS. MagicDNS can't hold custom records; Cloudflare is the record store.
  • Wildcard Let's Encrypt cert for the lab. zone via cert-manager DNS-01. The API token goes in cert-manager; the cert output in kube-system.
  • Sealed Secrets as the secrets layer, with the private-key backup rule and the existingSecret migration pattern.
  • Pattern B / multi-source GitOps conventions written down. Adopting kube-prom (as kube-prom) and ArgoCD into tracked Applications.
  • Orphan cleanup done; learned that deleting an Application ≠ pruning its resources.

docs.title: Still open (carried into next weeks)
docs.text:
• Grafana lab. IngressRoute is still hand-applied drift → needs to move to apps/monitoring-extras/.
  • MetalLB advertising the Traefik VIP on legion (.249 showed up as an EXTERNAL-IP), flagged as a risk at this point because legion was still thought of as transient. (This becomes acceptable once legion is confirmed always-on.)
  • Grafana admin password → SealedSecret migration (grafana.admin.existingSecret).
  • node-exporter DaemonSet on legion needs a toleration so a powered-down legion doesn't hold monitoring at Progressing.
  • kube-prom chart bump (85.0.2 → newer) deferred until after adoption.
  • Renovate still not set up.
  • The ArgoCD CRD annotations: Too long problem is looming (surfaces properly in Week 6).

docs.title: Week 9: First Real App, WireGuard Direct, Storage Hardware, and the Observability Grind
docs.text:
Covers roughly 2 – 8 July 2026.

This week had two threads running in parallel: getting the cluster genuinely ready for real applications (planning the portfolio site, sorting Longhorn hardware, root-access WireGuard), and a long, grinding observability buildout that surfaced a family of ArgoCD/CRD problems I'm still untangling.

docs.title: 1. Is the cluster ready for real apps? (Mostly yes)
docs.text:
I did a status check on the foundations. The verdict:

  • Ingress/TLS (Traefik + Cloudflare + cert-manager): done.
  • GitOps deploy pipeline (proven with nginx): done.
  • Sealed Secrets: done.
  • Longhorn (node-independent storage): still in progress, and it's the key blocker for stateful workloads.

Two things flagged as must-do-before-real-data: configure the Longhorn backup target (NFS on tank) before any database holds anything meaningful, and actually verify node-independent placement works before assuming a database can float across nodes.

docs.title: 2. The portfolio site: planning my first real application
docs.text:
I proposed a portfolio site (frontend + Go backend + database) as the first real app. This got endorsed as a strong first project: it does double duty as a deployment exercise and a Go learning vehicle, and the backend complexity is intentionally low (a few JSON endpoints) so I can focus on Go the language rather than distributed-systems correctness.

The deliberate sequencing decision: portfolio site before obsync. obsync layers Go + Postgres + a hand-written sync protocol all at once, too many new problems simultaneously. The portfolio site lets me learn the deployment shape with low stakes first.

How the pieces map to my patterns:

  • Frontend → built-from-source (Hugo/Astro noted earlier), its own repo + CI.
  • Go backend → built-from-source, its own repo + CI.
  • Postgres → off-the-shelf Pattern B (manifest + ArgoCD Application, no CI).

Left open at the time: the rendering approach: static frontend + separate Go JSON API, vs server-side rendering in Go (templ/html-template), vs an SPA calling a Go JSON API. (This gets picked up when I actually deploy Postgres in Week 7.)

docs.title: 3. WireGuard: finally, root access on the ONR
docs.text:
The big networking unblock. I found a root-level admin account on the Singtel ONR that exposes DHCP, static IP reservation, and port forwarding, the exact controls I'd been locked out of.

I sorted out a conceptual confusion first: IP routing (static routes between subnets) is not the same as port forwarding/NAT (exposing an internal host to the internet). I'd been conflating them. What I needed was port forwarding.

The exact rule: UDP, port 51820 external and internal, targeting deus (selectable directly from the ONR's client dropdown now that static reservations are done), on the correct WAN interface (1_TR069_INTERNET_R_VID_10). The prerequisite is verifying that interface carries the real public IP, not a carrier-NAT address. Definitive test: sudo wg show on deus from a device off the LAN (phone on mobile data) showing a completed handshake.

I paused to think about the security of opening a port, and came away reassured: forwarding a single UDP port to WireGuard is about the lowest-risk exposure there is. WireGuard is cryptographically silent to unauthenticated packets: indistinguishable from a closed port to a scanner, no banner, no fingerprint, minimal audited codebase. The residual risks are (1) key management on client devices (a phone with a WireGuard config is effectively a LAN key), and (2) not forwarding additional ports beyond the single WireGuard entry. Also worth confirming the ONR's stateful firewall stays active and the forward is an exception to it, not a symptom of a broader bypass.

End state of the network stack: Cloudflare Tunnel for public services (outbound-only), WireGuard on UDP 51820 for private high-throughput admin access. Both feeding Traefik.

docs.title: 4. Storage hardware: sourcing Longhorn disks
docs.text:
Longhorn can't use ZFS (established in Week 4), so I needed dedicated disks. I worked through three options for getting them:

  1. Claw back space from nebula's ZFS mirror: rejected. ZFS doesn't support in-place vdev shrinking, so this means either breaking the mirror (killing redundancy) or a full backup-destroy-restore with ongoing IOPS contention. Neither fits an architecture whose whole point is data safety.
  2. Buy new drives: the sensible default.
  3. Used drives: where I actually landed.

A couple of corrections I picked up while drive-shopping:

  • The WD Red SA500 is not DRAM-less (I'd initially thought so and corrected it); it uses a Marvell controller with TLC NAND and does have DRAM. It's a NAS-rated drive built for 24/7, which is a genuinely better replica posture than a consumer SSD.
  • NVMe M.2 drives use PCIe lanes, not SATA ports, so adding NVMe doesn't cost me a SATA port. NVMe is a real option, not a compromise.
  • The meaningful drive filter isn't "has DRAM" alone; it's "DRAM or HMB + TLC NAND." QLC is more harmful than DRAM-absence for sustained Longhorn replication writes.

Then the plan changed for the better: I got three used 256GB M.2 NVMe SSDs (Intel + WD, both with DRAM) for free from my company's IT department. 256GB is plenty per node since bulk data lives on ZFS. Plan: two drives across deus and nebula for replica count 2 (the redundancy floor), third as a cold spare.

(Note: this "deus + nebula" replica plan shifts again in Week 7; deus ends up with no replicas due to its overheating, so the targets become nebula + legion.)

I also worked out the used-drive validation workflow for the free SSDs: smartctl -a (watch Percentage Used, Available Spare, Media/Data Integrity Errors, Critical Warning) → non-destructive badblocks -sv → destructive badblocks -wsv to exercise every cell → re-read SMART to confirm no degradation. And verify which M.2 slots are actually free first: deus has only one M.2 slot and it may already hold the OS drive.

docs.title: 5. The observability grind
docs.text: The longest, most frustrating thread of the week. I was building a proper "Homelab: Node Overview" Grafana dashboard on kube-prometheus-stack (chart v85.0.2, release kube-prom, values in apps/monitoring/values-monitoring.yaml, managed as a multi-source ArgoCD Application).

docs.title: Getting metrics flowing
docs.text:
• Dashboard 237 was empty because of stale metric names: the imported dashboard referenced old names.
  • Enabled hardware temperature monitoring via the hwmon collector + coretemp kernel module.
  • Hit a many-to-one join error on node_hwmon_temp_celsius: the fix was joining on(chip, instance), not just on(chip). And I had to filter chip_name="coretemp" because max(node_hwmon_temp_celsius) was otherwise grabbing the hottest sensor of any hardware, not the CPU cores.
  • Confirmed chip names per node: all three have coretemp for CPU; nebula also has asus (eeepc_wmi) and nvme; deus has acpitz and nvme; legion has pch_cannonlake, iwlwifi_1, adp0.

docs.title: GPU metrics
docs.text: Set up nvidia_gpu_exporter (utkuozdemir, v1.2.1) as a Compose service on nebula (since the GTX 1080 lives on nebula, the Compose host). Metrics come out under the nvidia_smi_* prefix. Confirmed names: nvidia_smi_utilization_gpu_ratio (a ratio, needs * 100), nvidia_smi_temperature_gpu, nvidia_smi_power_draw_watts, nvidia_smi_memory_used_bytes / _total_bytes. To scrape a Compose service from in-cluster Prometheus, I made a ScrapeConfig CRD in a separate monitoring-extras ArgoCD Application, with a static instance="nebula" label that landed correctly on the GPU metrics. Built the unified dashboard with a $node template variable (CPU, RAM, temp, disk, network) plus a GPU row scoped to nebula.

docs.title: The ArgoCD CRD mess (still not fully resolved)
docs.text:
This is the ugly part, and it's a family of related problems:

  • I'm on ArgoCD v3.4.3, which has a known h2c port-forward bug making the CLI unreliable, which made everything else harder to debug.
  • A persistent ComparisonError on the kube-prom Application because readOnlyRootFilesystem wasn't in ArgoCD's client-side structured-merge diff schema.
  • App-level ServerSideApply=true collides with ArgoCD's controller-injected syncStrategy.apply.force: they're mutually exclusive at the apply level. A patch I tried that included syncStrategy.apply.force got stuck in the automated retry loop and had to be cleared by disabling automation, removing the /operation field, and re-syncing.
  • The session ended mid-resolution with the CRDs (thanosrulers, alertmanagers, prometheusagents, scrapeconfigs, alertmanagerconfigs, prometheuses) failing on metadata.annotations: Too long: may not be more than 262144 bytes, the canonical kube-prometheus-stack + ArgoCD problem, caused by client-side apply storing last-applied-configuration in an annotation that blows past the 262KB ceiling.

The end-state I identified (but hadn't fully committed): resource-level argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: ServerSideApply=true annotations on the CRDs (via crds.annotations) and the node-exporter DaemonSet (via daemonsetAnnotations), no app-level SSA, plus ignoreDifferences on the relevant fields. (This gets refined further in Week 7 when I discover the chart version doesn't even have a crds.annotations injection point.)

docs.title: 6. Reclaiming under-provisioned disk space
docs.text: A quick, useful find: every node only had ~100GB allocated to the OS despite larger disks. Classic Ubuntu Server LVM under-provisioning: the installer makes a volume group from the whole disk but only allocates part of it to the root LV. Fix: lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv then resize2fs (ext4) or xfs_growfs (XFS), both online-safe, no reboot. Since all three nodes share the install config, this is a prime candidate for a retroactive Ansible playbook.

docs.title: Week 10: Longhorn Disks Live, the Database Lands, and the Loose Ends Get Tied
docs.text:
Covers roughly 9 – 15 July 2026. This is the most recent week.

If Week 6 was "get ready," this week was "actually do it." The Longhorn disks went in, the observability CRD mess finally got resolved, the Grafana password loop got killed properly, and (the milestone) the first real database landed on the cluster via CloudNativePG, backups and all. Also confronted the uncomfortable truth that deus is a single point of failure.

docs.title: 1. Longhorn disks physically installed and configured
docs.text:
The free NVMe drives from Week 6 went in. Final storage topology, per node:

  • deus: 256GB NVMe is the OS drive; overheats; no Longhorn replicas. Scheduling disabled entirely; deus is compute/control only.
  • nebula: got a 256GB WDC PC SN730 NVMe dedicated entirely to Longhorn (no partitioning). Also has the 931.5G SSD and the two 3.6T ZFS pool drives, OS on sdd. Longhorn scheduling enabled only on the dedicated disk.
  • legion: got a 500GB WD Red SA500 SATA SSD (/dev/sda), partitioned: ~400G formatted ext4 directly (no LVM) at /var/lib/longhorn-disk-sda for Longhorn, ~65G as a separate spare-vg on /dev/sda2 for general use.

Key config points:

  • 2-replica, targets are nebula's SN730 + legion's WD Red partition, meaning zero placement slack with only two targets. (I corrected an earlier cached assumption that deus and nebula were the replica pair; deus has no replicas.)
  • On every node, the default /var/lib/longhorn OS-disk path is scheduling-disabled; only the dedicated disks schedule.
  • The WD Red SA500 being NAS-rated for 24/7 meaningfully improves the replica posture on legion.

A couple of hands-on gotchas installing the drives:

  • On nebula's NVMe, lsblk showed no partitions but mkfs.ext4 detected a leftover GPT table from the drive's previous life: had to wipefs -a /dev/nvme0n1 first. Correct sequence: wipefs -a → mkfs.ext4 -L longhorn-nebula → mkdir → blkid → fstab entry (by UUID, with nofail) → mount -a.
  • Interpreted the SMART check on the used NVMe: PASSED, 0 media/data integrity errors, 100% available spare, 20% wear (~33TB written), 857 unsafe shutdowns (cosmetic, not corruption). Healthy enough.

docs.title: 2. Bringing Longhorn itself under GitOps
docs.text: I adopted the existing Longhorn v1.12.0 Helm install into an ArgoCD Application without reinstalling: the diff showed only ArgoCD tracking-id annotation additions, no pod restarts, confirming a safe adoption. This is the same "adopt, don't reinstall" pattern I used for kube-prom in Week 5.

docs.title: 3. Killing the Grafana password loop for good
docs.text:
The Grafana admin password kept resetting on every ArgoCD sync. Root cause, stated cleanly: the Grafana Helm subchart generates a random password at helm template time, and selfHeal: true then stamps that over the live secret every reconcile. Any credential the Helm chart owns will churn under self-heal; that's the general principle.

The fix (finally committed this week): a SealedSecret named grafana-admin in apps/monitoring-extras/, with values-monitoring.yaml pointing at it via grafana.admin.existingSecret: grafana-admin (userKey: admin-user, passwordKey: admin-password). That removes password ownership from the Helm chart entirely and makes the SealedSecret the git-declared source of truth ArgoCD won't churn.

Two caveats I noted: Grafana only reads admin-password on first boot / DB init, so if the admin user already exists I may need grafana-cli admin reset-admin-password or a PVC wipe; and the Sealed Secrets private-key backup must be current before committing. The secret didn't appear at first but resolved on its own once the ArgoCD poll caught up, a timing issue, not a config error (a recurring theme, and an argument for finally fixing the webhook).

docs.title: 4. The ArgoCD CRD Too long problem: resolved
docs.text:
I finally closed out the CRD annotation mess from Week 6. Inspecting the actual chart tarball revealed the real situation: kube-prometheus-stack 85.0.2 ships its CRDs as raw untemplated files with no crds.annotations injection point, so the resource-level SSA-via-values approach I'd planned in Week 6 was impossible for this chart version.

The correct fix turned out to be simpler: the app-level ServerSideApply=true already sat in argocd/kube-prometheus-stack.yaml in Git; it just was never applied to the live cluster, because argocd/ isn't watched by any app-of-apps and requires a manual kubectl apply. So I applied that file and stripped the stale kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation off the six affected CRDs.

Then one last sync failure: failed to create typed patch object on the node-exporter DaemonSet, because readOnlyRootFilesystem was set inside the pod-level securityContext where it isn't a valid schema field. Client-side apply had silently tolerated it; SSA's strict schema enforcement surfaced it. Removed that one line (the chart's containerSecurityContext already sets it correctly by default).

The recurring structural lesson from all of this: the absence of an app-of-apps watching argocd/ is a silent-drift source in my setup: Application definitions committed to argocd/ don't take effect until I manually apply them. That's a real gap to close.

docs.title: 5. The database lands: CloudNativePG
docs.text:
The milestone of the week: the first real stateful workload. I deployed PostgreSQL via the CloudNativePG (CNPG) operator for the portfolio site.

The mental model that made it make sense was a two-layer control loop: ArgoCD owns the Cluster CR (the desired state in Git), and CNPG owns the actual pod/PVC/Secret (reconciling the database to match the CR). Decided strategically: Postgres-via-CNPG is the default for all K8s database workloads, one Cluster CR per application (not a shared instance), unless a workload ships its own embedded store.

Real issues diagnosed and fixed along the way:

  • CRD-not-found at first because I'd put the Cluster CR in argocd/cnpg.yaml instead of a proper Application CR.
  • kubectl apply structural error switching from source to sources (single- to multi-source): needed --server-side.
  • Port collision: the kubectl port-forward clashed with a Windows-installed PostgreSQL service on 5432.
  • pgAdmin instability over port-forward: port-forward just isn't suited to GUI clients holding persistent connections.
  • Backup credential error: I sealed the Garage key's friendly name (cnpg-key) instead of its actual key ID (GK...).
  • A kubectl ambiguity worth remembering: after adopting Longhorn, kubectl get backup resolves to backups.longhorn.io, not the CNPG resource, so I need kubectl get backups.postgresql.cnpg.io explicitly now.

docs.title: Backups: Garage over MinIO
docs.text: For CNPG's S3-compatible backup target I started with MinIO but switched to Garage after finding MinIO's community edition stripped access-key management from the UI after a mid-2025 product pivot. Garage went up via Docker Compose on nebula, data on tank/backups/garage (ZFS), replication_factor = 1, a cnpg-backups bucket granted to a dedicated key (garage key create + garage bucket allow). The CNPG Cluster CR got a barmanObjectStore pointing at http://192.168.1.248:3900, WAL compression on, and a ScheduledBackup CR for 3am daily.

docs.title: 6. Confronting the deus single point of failure
docs.text: Installing storage made me face that deus is a SPOF for the K3s control plane: single-server embedded etcd. I'm considering buying a mini PC. The important correction I absorbed: two K3s server nodes with embedded etcd is worse than one (no quorum, an even number can't break ties). Genuine control-plane HA needs three server nodes. So a single new mini PC is best used as a worker (to reduce blast radius and migrate pinned services off deus), not as a stepping stone to HA. The endgame framing: two or three dedicated mini PCs as the server/etcd tier, with the current nodes as workers.

docs.title: 7. Smaller things this week
docs.text:
• Dev container scale-to-zero. To turn code-server off when unused without self-heal fighting me: the clean answer is ignoreDifferences on /spec/replicas so "off" is the declared default and manual kubectl scale persists. replicas: 0 in Git gets reverted by self-heal; KEDA scale-to-zero is deferred (poorly suited to code-server's long-lived tunnel connection). Scale to zero is safe because the PVC (including tunnel auth at ~/.vscode/cli) persists across restarts.
  • Headlamp deployed via ArgoCD with a long-lived ServiceAccount token (headlamp-admin → cluster-admin), the chart's ingress disabled, replaced with a hand-authored Traefik IngressRoute at headlamp.lab.packetcraft.dev. This is where the ArgoCD-not-auto-syncing-on-push problem got pinned down: it's the missing GitHub webhook (poll-interval lag). The webhook is the clean fix, contingent on the ArgoCD UI already being exposed through the tunnel.
  • Kubernetes dashboard chase. Tried to add the official kubernetes-dashboard; its Helm repo 404'd and I burned time chasing non-existent OCI/GHCR paths (all 403'd) before web search confirmed the HTTP repo is still the documented method. Pivoted to evaluating kite (kite-org/kite) instead: actively maintained, but a much heavier platform tool with write capabilities, an AI agent that can mutate the cluster, and a SQLite+PVC requirement. If I deploy kite it must stay on the tailnet plane (*.lab.packetcraft.dev) given those mutation powers. Left undecided pending read-only-vs-read-write scoping and whether to enable the AI agent. (Headlamp is the lighter option I actually deployed.)
  • Regenerated the Docker and K3s guides to be generalized/reusable rather than project-specific, keeping some first-person voice in the K3s one for the genuinely non-obvious bits (the SSH-localhost trap, taint+toleration as attraction+permission, tunnel ingress as one pattern among several).
  • Secrets manager question settled again: Sealed Secrets is enough; no Vault / ESO until I need dynamic secrets, rotation, or audit logging.
